magic-the-gathering.context_blurb:
Magic: the Gathering reached shops in August 1993, the first trading-card game anybody had made: build a deck, tap lands for mana, drag your opponent from twenty life to zero.

A mathematics professor designed it: Richard Garfield. His Pennsylvania doctorate was in combinatorial mathematics, the branch that counts arrangements and analyses games. In 1991 he took it to a garage company in Renton, Washington, started a year earlier by a Boeing programmer: Wizards of the Coast, founded by Peter Adkison. Adkison had wanted to print another Garfield design first, the robot-programming board game RoboRally, but it cost too much. Garfield's rule was that three cards drawn at random ought to add up to a plan, an idea from a 1977 board game where each player's alien breaks one rule: Cosmic Encounter.

Mana comes in five colours — white, blue, black, red and green — for law, knowledge, ambition, passion and nature. Each colour has two allies beside it on the wheel and two enemies across from it. White's enemies are black and red. Turning a card ninety degrees to show it is used, a land for mana or a creature attacking, is tapping; it straightens up next turn. A creature cannot attack the turn it arrives unless it has haste: summoning sickness, there to stop first-turn kills.

The one-mana red spell that throws three damage at any target is Lightning Bolt. The two-mana blue spell that cancels another spell outright is Counterspell. The five-mana white angel with four power, flying and vigilance, is Serra Angel. The one-mana green flyer that taps for any colour is Birds of Paradise. Of the moxen, stones that tap for one colour each, the white one is Mox Pearl.

Alpha, the first run, came to about 2.6 million cards; collectors tell it from Beta by its rounder corners. Beta sharpened them, and December's third run, Unlimited, traded the black borders for white. One dual land, Volcanic Island, was left off the Beta sheets and not reprinted until Revised in 1994, so its Alpha copies are the rarest of the duals. Adkison, nearly broke, drove to the printing plant himself for the first boxes, in Carthage, Tennessee.

The first expansion, that December, took its djinns and sultans from the Thousand and One Nights: Arabian Nights. March 1994's artifact set told of two brothers whose war cooled the planet into an ice age: Urza and Mishra. June brought a 310-card monster, the biggest set yet, with multicolour cards, banding and the legendary type: Legends. Its five eight-mana Elder Dragons each wanted three coloured mana every upkeep or had to be given up, so only a mana-rich deck could hold one. The horned blue-black-red dragon became the game's standing villain for thirty years: Nicol Bolas. The same set gave us the land restricted to one copy for bouncing any legendary creature, Karakas. Its priciest card is The Tabernacle at Pendrell Vale, a legendary land charging every creature's owner a mana each upkeep.

The first World Championship ran at Gen Con in Milwaukee in August 1994, where sixteen-year-old Zak Dolan won on the back of an artifact creature, Su-Chi. Bertrand Lestree, the Frenchman he beat, is remembered for the opposite plan: huge green creatures and forest acceleration behind Erhnam Djinn. The first Pro Tour followed in New York in February 1996 with a hundred thousand dollars in prizes, and Michael Loconto won it with a swarm of cheap white creatures. Wizards had barred the Alpha rarities, the Power Nine among them, so that old collections could not buy the title.

One Alpha sorcery turned life into colourless mana and, with Fireball, killed on turn one; it was restricted rather than banned: Channel. Eight of the Power Nine appeared only in 1993, but Time Vault carried on through Revised and Fourth Edition. In July 1995 a cheap white-bordered compilation reprinted the best of the early expansions, crashed the collector market and enraged the players: Chronicles. Wizards left Mishra's Workshop out of Chronicles in 1995 on purpose, knowing what it could do at a tournament, and no reprint exists. The Reserved List arrived in April 1996 as a promise never to reprint, and in 2002 Wizards took the commons and uncommons off it, keeping the rares. Christopher Rush, who painted Black Lotus, spent his last years signing cards at conventions; collectors call them Rush Lotuses. One signed copy, graded gem mint, sold in January 2021 for around $511,000. Magic's first comics came from Armada Comics.

pro-wrestling-wwf-wwe.context_blurb:
From 1984 to 2002, two companies ran wrestling.

Hulk Hogan called his arms his pythons and tore off yellow shirts. His finish: a big boot, then the leg drop. Vince McMahon poached him from Verne Gagne's AWA in 1983. The man first slated to lose the belt to him was Don Muraco. The neon-sunglassed elbow-dropper with Miss Elizabeth was Randy Savage. The black-coated Deadman unbeaten at WrestleMania is the Undertaker. That spring show, held yearly since 1985, is WrestleMania. The first one teamed Hogan with a star of Rocky III: Mr. T.

At WrestleMania III Hogan slammed the giant who played Fezzik, Andre the Giant. Andre had turned on him by ripping his crucifix off, drawing blood. In the semi-main, Ricky Steamboat took the Intercontinental belt from Savage. At WrestleMania VI the Ultimate Warrior beat Hogan and merged the WWF and Intercontinental titles.

The Calgary Hitman in pink and black is Bret Hart. He lost the Intercontinental belt at Wembley to his brother-in-law, the British Bulldog. At Montreal in 1997 McMahon had the bell rung on Bret's own hold, the Sharpshooter. The documentary caught Bret spitting on McMahon from inside the ring before the bell. Afterwards Bret punched him backstage, and McMahon hurt his ankle in the fall.

The Heartbreak Kid, with Sweet Chin Music for a finish, is Shawn Michaels. A herniated disc in his back kept him out for four years. Five friends broke the oldest rule by hugging onstage: Shawn Michaels, Razor Ramon, Diesel and Hunter Hearst Helmsley, who is Triple H. D-Generation X asked if you were ready and answered itself: suck it. Triple H's double-underhook facebuster is the Pedigree, a word meaning pure aristocratic ancestry, as in a thoroughbred horse.

WCW fired young Steve Austin by FedEx while he healed from surgery. Beating Jake Roberts in 1996, he mocked the preacher's verse and took the numbers 3:16, as Austin 3:16. His first shirt was black with white block letters and no skull. His finish, a gut kick and a jaw across his shoulder, is the Stone Cold Stunner.

The eyebrow-raising third-generation star asking what he was cooking is the Rock. His insult jabroni comes from the wrestler whose work is losing, a jobber. He won his first title when McMahon switched sides to help him cheat, founding the Corporation. At WrestleMania X-Seven McMahon helped Austin beat him, turning Austin heel, and the show closed with Austin toasting McMahon with two beers. In Toronto the crowd cheered Hogan, the scripted villain, and booed the Rock, so the two called audibles in the ring to swap spots for him.

Mike Tyson worked WrestleMania XIV as the main event's outside enforcer, for a reported three million dollars. Mick Foley's masked, drooling boiler-room character with the sock puppet is Mankind. The Undertaker threw him off the sixteen-foot cell through the Spanish announce table, then put him through the roof of the cage into the ring, and a tooth ended up in his nose, pulled out later with pliers. He wrote his memoir in pencil in notebooks on coach flights. Kane debuted in red and black as the Undertaker's storyline half-brother. When Foley won the title on a taped Raw, Nitro spoiled it live, read out by Tony Schiavone. Eric Bischoff ordered it, thinking nobody would care and that it would keep his own audience. The countdown clock that interrupted the Rock in 1999 was Y2J, Chris Jericho.

Ted Turner's Atlanta company, eighty-three weeks ahead in the ratings, was WCW. Nitro opened in 1995 with Sting attacking his own ally Hogan. Hogan turned on his own side to stand with Kevin Nash and Scott Hall as the third man in the New World Order. The WWF had sued over those gimmicks, claiming trademark infringement. Sting's white face paint and rafter-bat were copied from The Crow. Goldberg's streak ended when Hall used a hidden stun gun and the pin went to Kevin Nash. Kurt Angle's 1996 gold, won on a broken neck, came in freestyle wrestling at heavyweight. Eddie Guerrero's three words were lie, cheat and steal. His father Gory ran a promotion from the 1940s in El Paso, Texas. Chyna won the Intercontinental title from Jeff Jarrett in a Good Housekeeping match. Bruno Sammartino held the belt nearly eight years until Ivan Koloff, the Russian Bear, pinned him. The Philadelphia bingo-hall promotion of barbed wire and tables, booked by Paul Heyman, was ECW, and the man who founded the Japanese deathmatch company FMW in 1989 is Atsushi Onita.

seattle-seahawks.context_blurb:
Seattle joined the National Football League in 1976 as an expansion club, played in the Kingdome until 1999 and now plays indoors at Lumen Field in blue, green and silver. The team is the Seahawks, and its crowd has shaken a seismograph more than once.

The first great player was a receiver out of Tulsa whom nobody wanted, judged too small and too slow, who spent fourteen years in Seattle and retired in 1989 holding every career record for catches, yards and touchdowns: Steve Largent. He went to Congress in 1994 for Oklahoma's first district. The left tackle who started for twelve seasons from 1997, made nine Pro Bowls and never played for another club was Walter Jones. The defensive tackle who stayed unblockable on a two-win team in 1992 took the league's honour for the best defender in the game that year, which made Cortez Kennedy the NFL Defensive Player of the Year.

Shaun Alexander ran for 1,880 yards and twenty-eight touchdowns in 2005 and was voted the league's most valuable player. Pittsburgh then beat Seattle 21-10 in the Super Bowl in a game full of calls that all went one way, and years later the referee Bill Leavy stood up at Seahawks training camp and admitted he had kicked two of them and that it had haunted him since.

In 2010 the Seahawks hired a grinning, gum-chewing coach out of the University of Southern California: Pete Carroll. He replaced a man who had lasted a single 5-11 season, Jim Mora. Carroll inherited the running back newly arrived from Buffalo who called himself Beast Mode and ate Skittles on the sideline: Marshawn Lynch. On 8 January 2011, against New Orleans in the playoffs, Lynch broke nine tackles over sixty-seven yards for a touchdown, and the noise of the crowd showed up on a University of Washington seismograph, which is how the run got its name: the Beast Quake. It read about magnitude two. The piece everybody replays is the flat-palm stiff-arm he planted in Tracy Porter's facemask, lifting the man off his feet and backwards.

Carroll's secondary hit hard enough to earn a name of its own, because Kam Chancellor, Earl Thomas, Richard Sherman and Brandon Browner together were the Legion of Boom. In 2013 they gave up 172.0 passing yards a game, the lowest figure in the league since 1997. In the conference championship that January, Sherman tipped a fade away from Michael Crabtree at the back of the end zone and Malcolm Smith caught the deflection.

The quarterback was a third-round pick, seventy-fifth overall, who had moved to Wisconsin for his final college year after being passed over at NC State: Russell Wilson. Seattle had just paid twenty-six million dollars for a free agent to play that position, Matt Flynn, and Wilson beat him out in camp. Wilson led the rout of Denver in Super Bowl XLVIII, 43-8, in February 2014, and was traded to those same Broncos in 2022. The first play from scrimmage in that game ended with the ball sailing over Peyton Manning's head into his own end zone: a safety twelve seconds in, the fastest score the Super Bowl has ever produced.

A year later Seattle lost the rematch by a yard. With twenty-six seconds left and the ball on the one, Darrell Bevell, the offensive coordinator, called for a slant rather than a run, explaining afterwards that he wanted to save the clock and not get stuck on third down, and an undrafted rookie out of West Alabama stepped in front of the pass: Malcolm Butler. New England had that same goal-line slant on film from earlier in the playoff run, which is why Butler jumped it.

Lynch spent that Super Bowl week answering every question with one repeated sentence, telling the reporters he was only there so he would not get fined.

After Wilson's trade, the backup nobody expected anything from led the whole league in accuracy in 2022, completing 69.8 percent of his passes: Geno Smith.

seattle-mariners.context_blurb:
The Mariners arrived as an expansion club in 1977, played indoors in the concrete Kingdome, and moved outdoors in 1999 to Safeco Field, now T-Mobile Park. The glory years run from 1989 to 2001.

The centre fielder with the sweetest swing in baseball hit fifty-six home runs in 1997 and wore his cap backwards on the cover of Sports Illustrated: Ken Griffey Jr. He had been the first pick of the 1987 draft and reached the majors at nineteen. In 1995 he tied the record for home runs in eight straight games, but earlier that season he hit the Kingdome wall at full speed making a catch and broke his left wrist, which cost him half a year. His father joined the club in 1990, and on 14 September the pair did something no father and son had managed in a major-league game before: they hit home runs back to back in the same inning. Voted into the Hall of Fame in 2016, Griffey took 99.3 percent of the ballots, 437 out of 440, missing a clean sweep by three writers who have never explained themselves. Seattle had traded him to Cincinnati in 2000, at his own request, for Mike Cameron, Brett Tomko, Antonio Perez and Jake Meyer.

The designated hitter who batted .312 across eighteen years in Seattle got a street beside the ballpark named for him and a place in the Hall of Fame in 2019: Edgar Martinez. The league renamed its yearly prize for the best designated hitter the Edgar Martinez Award.

On 8 October 1995, in the eleventh inning of the deciding game against the Yankees, Edgar lined a double into the left-field corner off Jack McDowell. Joey Cora scored from third and Griffey came the whole way from first, sliding in head-first; analysis of the broadcast film puts his run at about nine and a half seconds. Dave Niehaus told the radio audience that the Mariners were going to play for the American League championship, and then said the three words Seattle still repeats: my oh my. That hit is credited with keeping baseball in the city and paying for the new ballpark.

The six-foot-ten left-hander they called the Big Unit threw the first no-hitter in club history, against Detroit in 1990: Randy Johnson. Seattle had got him out of Montreal in 1989 by giving up its own left-handed ace, Mark Langston. The Venezuelan right-hander for whom a whole bleacher section dressed in yellow, the King's Court, pitched a perfect game against Tampa Bay in 2012: Felix Hernandez. He struck out twelve, the last of them Sean Rodriguez, swinging, and his was the third perfect game of that one season, after Philip Humber's and Matt Cain's.

The Japanese right fielder who crossed the Pacific in 2001 was voted both the league's best rookie and its most valuable player in one summer: Ichiro Suzuki. He added a Gold Glove and a Silver Slugger to the pair of them. In 2004 he passed George Sisler's eighty-four-year-old mark of 257 and finished the year on 262 hits. Rod Barajas, catching for Texas, walked out to first base to shake the hand of the man who had just broken it. Counting his nine seasons with the Orix BlueWave, he retired with 4,367 hits in all, 1,278 of them in Japan and 3,089 in America.

The 2001 team won 116 games, tying a total set in 1906 by the Chicago Cubs, and then lost the championship series to the Yankees anyway. Pat Gillick had built that side after losing Griffey and Alex Rodriguez: besides Ichiro he signed a second baseman who batted .331 that year with thirty-seven home runs and 141 runs driven in, Bret Boone. The year before, the 2000 side had also reached the championship series and also lost it to the Yankees, four games to two.

Seinfeld made a Mariner famous by accident, when Frank Costanza screams at George Steinbrenner about trading Jay Buhner away. The Yankees really did send Buhner to Seattle in 1988, and what they took back for him was the ageing Ken Phelps.

The drought that followed 2001 ran twenty-one years, the longest in the four major North American sports, and it ended on 30 September 2022 when the rookie catcher Cal Raleigh hit a walk-off home run against Oakland.

anime-dragon-ball.context_blurb:
Akira Toriyama started Dragon Ball in Weekly Shonen Jump in 1984: a boy alone in the mountains, black hair in spikes, a monkey tail, a red-tipped power pole, holding an orange ball with four stars in it that his late Grandpa Gohan left him, and the series named for those balls is Dragon Ball. The boy is Son Goku. Toriyama built him from Sun Wukong of Journey to the West, which is where the tail, staff and surname come from. His previous comic, a 1980 gag series about a robot girl called Arale built by a bumbling inventor in Penguin Village, is Dr. Slump.

A blue-haired teenager arrives on a motorbike with a radar that pings near the orbs, and she is Bulma. Her father founded Capsule Corp; Toriyama named the family after underwear. Holding all seven balls is not sufficient by itself, because the wish needs calling the dragon Shenron by name with all seven balls together. Afterwards they scatter and go inert for a year.

Being a Saiyan has consequences. Under a full moon Goku's tail turns him into a giant ape called the Oozaru, hundreds of feet tall, ten times stronger and almost mindless. Dragon Ball Z opens with his brother Raditz, and the old enemy turned ally who fires his Special Beam Cannon through both brothers while Goku holds Raditz in place, dying with them, is Piccolo.

Namek is where the series became what people remember. The tyrant Frieza kills Goku's oldest friend, the short bald monk Krillin, in front of him, and what detonates Goku's rage is Frieza killing Krillin in front of him. His hair goes gold and his eyes green in a form unseen for a thousand years, the Super Saiyan. The manga gives the planet five minutes to live; the anime, waiting on Toriyama's pages, stretched that into roughly 19 episodes, spread across about half a year of weekly broadcast.

Then Dr. Gero's bio-android arrives, built from the cells of every fighter, needing two earlier models to reach his perfect form, and the two he hunts are Androids 17 and 18, the twin siblings. A teenaged Trunks had already come back from a future in which Goku died of a heart virus, carrying a specific anti-heart-virus pharmaceutical from the future, in a Capsule Corp medicine bottle. Father and son train for the fight in the Hyperbolic Time Chamber above Korin Tower, where a day is a year and trainees get two cumulative days (two years of training) total per person across their lifetime. At the Cell Games Goku steps aside and sends his son in, because Goku has determined Gohan has greater untapped potential and a hidden form Cell hasn't seen. When Cell crushes Android 16 mid-sentence, Gohan ascends to Super Saiyan 2.

The Buu saga keeps the jokes running. The world champion who claims Gohan's victory for himself is a parody of a bombastic Western pro wrestler, with a name riffing on Hulk Hogan. Fat Buu befriends him and his dog, and the dog is Bee. The champion then redeems himself by talking the whole planet into raising its arms for Goku's borrowed-energy attack, The Spirit Bomb (Genki Dama).

Two production stories matter. Toriyama's editor Kazuhiko Torishima took to the Super Saiyan idea at once and let it through with almost no editorial changes. And the anime-only Red Ribbon detour had already produced a classic Toriyama trick, in which the cat sage at the top of Korin Tower makes Goku strong by promising him The Sacred Water, which turns out to have been a Karin Tower trick to make Goku train.

On television, Toei's 1986 opening was Makafushigi Adventure!, and the 1989 Z theme sung by Hironobu Kageyama is Cha-La Head-Cha-La. Toei rebuilt the show for its twentieth anniversary as Kai, cutting 291 episodes to about 167, and the work was Toei Animation in-house, with new dubbing and a re-edit by Kazuhiro Furuhashi. In English, one Funimation actor carried Vegeta, Piccolo, Yamcha and Master Roshi at once, and he is Christopher Sabat. Goku reached English first through the 1996 Ocean dub in Canada, where Ian Corlett began the role and Peter Kelamis took it over partway through, before Sean Schemmel won it in 1999. Vegeta's scouter reads over eight thousand in the Japanese, and the nine-thousand version everybody quotes came in with the English dub, so the real reading is Eight thousand. Dragon Ball GT, having no manga to follow, invented a red-furred form called Super Saiyan 4.

studio-ghibli.context_blurb:
Studio Ghibli grew out of one film made before it existed: a 1984 story of a poisoned future world and a princess who rides the wind and defends the giant insects everyone else fears, named for her, Nausicaa. She scouts the toxic forest on a one-seater jet glider called a Mehve, from the German word for seagull. Its success paid for the studio itself, set up in Tokyo in 1985 by Hayao Miyazaki, by the producer Toshio Suzuki, and by an older director who had been Miyazaki's mentor at Toei, Isao Takahata.

Takahata's 1988 film about a boy and his small sister starving in firebombed Kobe is Grave of the Fireflies, and the two children are Seita and Setsuko. It went out as a double bill with Miyazaki's countryside story of two sisters, Satsuki and Mei, who meet a huge grey forest spirit at a bus stop in the rain: My Neighbor Totoro, and the spirit is Totoro. Because Ghibli only animated the Takahata war film, that was the one title left out of the 1996 Disney agreement which carried the rest of the studio into American homes. Takahata also made the 1991 film in which a Tokyo office worker of twenty-seven goes to harvest safflowers and keeps remembering her fifth-grade self, Taeko Okajima.

Miyazaki's 1989 film sends a witch of thirteen away for her year alone, flying parcels over a seaside town, and she is Kiki. Her black cat is Jiji. His 1992 film puts a flying ace with a pig's face into a crimson seaplane above the Adriatic: Porco Rosso. His 2008 one gives a small boy a goldfish girl in a bucket, Ponyo. Every wave in it was drawn by hand, one frame at a time, in coloured pencil, and left unsmoothed, because he wanted them to behave like living creatures rather than fluid simulation. In the 2004 castle film the fire demon burning in the hearth, who walks the castle on a bargain with the wizard, is Calcifer, and in the English dub he was largely improvised by Billy Crystal. That film also holds the most-studied cooking scene in the studio, Howl frying bacon and eggs for Sophie and Markl over Calcifer's flame.

The 1986 flying-island film took its name from Gulliver's Travels, and Disney quietly dropped the word Laputa for the 2003 English release because in Spanish it is coarse slang for a prostitute.

Princess Mononoke, in 1997, follows a young Emishi prince cursed by a maddened boar god and riding west on a red elk: Ashitaka. The white wolf-god who raised San is Moro. The film broke every Japanese box-office record and held first place until Titanic arrived later that year. It was also the studio's first real experiment with computers, used on the black tentacles of the demon boar and on the boar charge later, though only about a tenth of the finished shots carried any digital work. Miramax took it to America, and when Harvey Weinstein pressed for cuts, Toshio Suzuki posted him a katana with a note reading no cuts. The English script was written by Neil Gaiman, the cursed boar god of the opening was voiced by Keith David, and Miyazaki picked the actress for Lady Eboshi himself: Minnie Driver.

The 2001 film about a girl of ten whose mother and father are turned into pigs, and who scrubs floors in a bathhouse for gods, is Spirited Away. Miyazaki draws his own boards as he directs, and he started that one with only about thirty percent of the story worked out. The witch who owns the bathhouse and steals letters out of the girl's name is Yubaba, and her gentler identical twin at the end of the one-way train line is Zeniba. On that journey the station signs are written in old right-to-left Japanese, which puts the whole ride in another era.

Two people made the studio look the way it looks. The watercolour backgrounds from 1988 onward were the work of the art director Kazuo Oga, and the fat Totoro silhouette on the logo was Toshio Suzuki's marketing idea, pushed through over Miyazaki's objection.

neon-genesis-evangelion.context_blurb:
Hideaki Anno made Neon Genesis Evangelion at Studio Gainax in 1995, and for a while it looks like a robot show. A cataclysm remembered as the Second Impact has already killed much of the world; what survives is run out of a bunker under Tokyo-3 by a United Nations agency called Nerv; and the enormous geometric things that keep arriving to finish the job are met by three teenagers strapped inside biomechanical giants. Nobody in the series calls the attackers aliens or monsters. They are Angels, and each one is named for a Judeo-Christian angel: Sachiel, Shamshel, Ramiel, Israfel, Sandalphon.

The pilots are not heroes. Shinji Ikari climbs into Unit 01 because his father tells him to, the redhead Asuka Langley takes Unit 02 out of pride, and the prototype, Unit 00, belongs to a pale girl with blue hair, red eyes and almost no expression, the First Child: Rei Ayanami. Yoshiyuki Sadamoto designed her, and half the anime of the following decade copied the design. Megumi Hayashibara, one of the busiest voices in Japan, who had spent the preceding years shouting as the sorceress Lina Inverse in Slayers, is the voice of Rei Ayanami.

The Christian furniture is everywhere: the angel names, the spear out of the crucifixion story called the Lance of Longinus, a Tree of Life diagram glowing in the command centre. Anno grew up in a household with no Christianity in it, and when interviewers pressed him his reason turned out to be purely visual: the imagery looked cool, and it looked nothing like the Japanese motifs everyone else was using. The diagram itself was lifted from a seventeenth-century book by the Jesuit polymath Athanasius Kircher, his Oedipus Aegyptiacus, which tried to read Egyptian hieroglyphs through Christian Kabbalah.

In March 1996 the final two episodes dropped the plot altogether for the pilots' inner monologue, played over half-finished pencil sketches and screens of black text, because Gainax had run out of both money and time. The fans were furious. A complete replacement ending reached cinemas that July, and before it, in March 1997, Gainax put out a stopgap that stitched a clip-show recap onto the first twenty-seven minutes of that new ending and called it Death and Rebirth.

Sadamoto drew his own comic version of the story as well. He started it in 1994, before the series was even broadcast, kept at it between other jobs, and published the fourteenth and final volume in June 2013. Yoshiyuki Sadamoto had come up through Tokyo's work for American television, storyboarding the title sequences of Thundercats and Silverhawks at Pacific Animation Corporation years before Evangelion made his name. The sword swinging into the camera and the beams crossing behind it in that cat-warrior opening are his.

Gainax itself started with a two-minute cartoon. In 1981 a group of Osaka students built a short for the opening ceremony of a science-fiction convention, Daicon III, in which a girl in a bunny suit cuts her way through the creatures of classic science fiction, and the hall went up like a firework. The girl is drawn in Hideaki Anno's own style, with key animation from Hiroyuki Yamaga and Takami Akai. Anno has said he poured his own depression into every frame of the series that followed.

cowboy-bebop.context_blurb:
Cowboy Bebop is twenty-six episodes made at Sunrise in 1998 and directed by Shinichiro Watanabe, about bounty hunters working the solar system in 2071 out of a battered ship called the Bebop. Watanabe's pitch named two American genres of the mid-century as the show's parents, film noir and the western, and the show is exactly that, since a bounty board is a western device while the lighting and the fatalism are noir. Spike himself is built out of Bruce Lee and 1970s Hong Kong cinema.

The crew is a lanky former syndicate hitman called Spike, a gruff ex-policeman named Jet with a prosthetic arm, the con-woman Faye, a barefoot child hacker called Edward, and a dog. The dog is a data dog, a genetically enhanced Pembroke Welsh corgi cleverer than most of the humans, and his name is Ein. The creators kept Ed's gender deliberately hard to read through voice and clothes and manner, and what they have said about the character is that Ed is Female, but with androgynous presentation.

The music is why people who do not watch anime watch this. Yoko Kanno wrote around eighty pieces for the run and fronts the studio band that plays them, a band named for the thing drivers are told to put on, The Seatbelts. The opening is a big-band blast with its title flashing up in one word, Tank! A walking bass drives it, the melody belongs to the tenor saxophone, and the horns are arranged to clash cheerfully with a cyberpunk future. Mai Yamane sang many of the vocal tracks.

The credits look as deliberate as they sound. The design borrows from the mid-century American title designer who made the sequences for Hitchcock, Preminger and Kubrick, and the trick is Saul Bass-inspired silhouetted figures against blocks of solid color, with hand-typeset character cards.

Spike's past is the thread under the comedy. He belonged to an elite unit of a crime organisation called the Red Dragon Syndicate and faked his death to get out, and the colleague from that unit who comes back for him is Vicious. His left eye is an implant from that old life, and he jokes that one eye sees the present and one sees the past; no single episode is built around how he lost it, and the episode fans point to is Episode 17, Mushroom Samba — though the eye is briefly referenced in the Ballad of Fallen Angels flashback. The two closing episodes borrow their title from a blues song, and the last of them is The Real Folk Blues, Part 2.

Getting the whole thing onto television took two tries. TV Tokyo found the violence and the tone too much and aired only half the run in 1998, and the full twenty-six went out uncut on the satellite channel WOWOW from October 1998 to April 1999. WOWOW did the same service for other adult anime of the period, and in 2001 Bebop crossed to America on Cartoon Network's Adult Swim, where for a great many viewers it was the first anime plainly made for grown-ups.

berserk.context_blurb:
Kentaro Miura published a Berserk prototype in 1988, began the serial in 1989, and drew it almost without a break until he died suddenly in May 2021, aged fifty-four, leaving one of the longest and most ferociously detailed epics anybody has attempted in comics. The world is a medieval Europe of mercenary bands, kings and demons. The hero is a huge scarred swordsman, branded for sacrifice and hunted by demons after dark, and his name is Guts. The sword he carries is a slab of iron almost as tall as he is, forged by the old blacksmith Godo for a king who wanted something a dragon could fall on, and it is called The Dragonslayer. Godo swore no human would ever swing it.

The spine of the series is a long flashback called the Golden Age, in which the young Guts fights for a rising mercenary army, the Band of the Hawk. Its commander is beautiful, golden-haired and set on owning a kingdom of his own one day, and he is Griffith. Casca, his second in command, loves him quietly. Miura spent volumes three to fourteen on this arc and treated it as the real story. Griffith has kept a charm since boyhood, a little crimson egg of stone whose eyes, nose and mouth sit jumbled across its shell as though a face had been shaken apart, and it is called the Behelit. Charms of the same kind keep surfacing all through the story, and fans know Griffith's own as the Egg of the King.

Miura assembled his hero out of things he loved, among them his high-school friend Kouji Mori and Mad Max's wasteland driver, while Guts's iron prosthetic hand came from Hyakkimaru in Osamu Tezuka's Dororo and the hero of the manga Cobra. Above all he named one actor, whose hard men in Flesh and Blood, Blade Runner and The Hitcher went into the making of the swordsman: Rutger Hauer.

The anime came in waves. Oriental Light and Magic made a twenty-five-episode television anime in 1997 that covered the Golden Age. Susumu Hirasawa's electronic score, shaped by his work with the band P-Model, is famous in its own right, above all the track Forces, which came out as a single. Studio 4C retold the arc as a trilogy of films in 2012 and 2013, with Hirasawa scoring again; a computer-animated series in 2016 tried to carry the story further and was never forgiven for how it looked.

Miura's own apprenticeship was short: at eighteen he went to assist George Morikawa, later the creator of the boxing epic Hajime no Ippo, and Morikawa soon sent him off, saying there was nothing left that he could teach the boy. A few years later the forty-eight-page Berserk prototype won a prize in Hakusensha's ComiComi contest. Miura's last completed chapter was 364, in volume 41. His friend from high school Kouji Mori, who writes Holyland and says Miura told him the whole ending in detail, has carried the manga on since June 2022 with the assistants of Studio Gaga.

mobile-suit-gundam.context_blurb:
Mobile Suit Gundam reached Japanese television in 1979 and quietly killed off the super-robot cartoon. The giant machines in it are army equipment: they overheat, they run dry of ammunition, and the people hauling on the levers are teenagers conscripted into a war between Earth and a breakaway colony state. The man who built that universe, nicknamed by fans for how freely he kills his own characters, is Yoshiyuki Tomino.

The rookie at the controls of the white, red and blue hero machine, model RX-78-2, is Amuro Ray, and he spends the series being hunted by a Zeon ace in a half-mask whose crimson suit invented the rule that an ace flies a custom colour: Char Aznable. The name he was born with is Casval Rem Deikun. The hardware itself, the Gundam and the Zaku and the Gouf and the Zeong, came from the first dedicated mechanical designer the industry ever had, Kunio Okawara.

The show failed on air. Its network cut the run short, and what rescued it was reruns plus a box of plastic: in July 1980 Bandai put snap-together kits on sale that let a kid build his own RX-78-2 on the kitchen table, the 1/144 scale Gunpla line, and the first batch sold out in hours. A business now worth billions grew out of model sprues, and the 1981 trilogy of cinema recuts finally handed the story a mass audience.

America met the franchise through Gundam Wing, which aired in Japan in 1995 and became one of the earliest draws on Cartoon Network's Toonami block in March 2000. It sends a squad of colony boys down to break the Earth Alliance's war, and the number of Gundam pilots in that squad is five. Sunrise restarted the idea in 2002 with Gundam Seed, a war between ordinary humans and the genetically engineered Coordinators, whose conflicted teenage hero flies the Strike Gundam and is called Kira Yamato.

akira.context_blurb:
Akira opens with a silent white blast erasing Tokyo in 1988 and then jumps thirty years forward into Neo-Tokyo, a neon megacity built on the crater, where bike gangs race through the streets and the army keeps psychic children in a laboratory. The man who wrote and drew the enormous manga it comes from directed the film as well, and he is Katsuhiro Otomo. His comic had been running in Young Magazine since 1982; he made the film halfway through it and changed the comic's ending afterwards.

The story turns on two friends. Tetsuo Shima crashes his bike, disappears into a military lab and comes back with powers nobody can hold; the leader of their gang, who spends the film chasing him through the city, is Kaneda. His red motorcycle is the most copied machine in animation.

Everything about the production was excessive for 1988. Otomo insisted the mouths be drawn to match voices already recorded, which reversed the usual order of work in anime, and more than 160,000 cels went into it, over twice the usual count. The money came from a consortium including Bandai, Kodansha and Toho, and the budget was approximately 11 million dollars, nearly double the previous record for Japanese animation. The jet-turbine howl of Kaneda's bike was never a jet at all, since it came from a modified Kawasaki Ninja motorcycle, recorded on a closed Tokyo street, and was then layered under drums.

The score is the other reason nobody forgets the film. Geinoh Yamashirogumi, an ensemble of university colleagues and amateur singers, recorded most of it before the animation existed, so the pictures were cut to fit the music, and the three sounds it was built from are taiko drums, Indonesian gamelan, and traditional Japanese noh chanting. The opening is one headlight in the dark, and then the title slams in on the drums.

Akira reached American cinemas on 25 December 1989 through Streamline Pictures, and for a generation of Western viewers it was the proof that animation could be serious and adult and frightening. Pioneer made a fresh English dub in 2001 with a new cast, Joshua Seth playing Tetsuo and Kaneda going to a voice actor familiar to anyone who watched Power Rangers: Johnny Yong Bosch. The sideways stop of the red bike has since been quoted in Ready Player One, in Chronicle, in Looper, in a Kanye West video and in the Spider-Verse sequel, so most people have seen the shot before they ever see the film.

ghost-in-the-shell.context_blurb:
Masamune Shirow began the Ghost in the Shell manga in 1989, and Production I.G made the film in 1995. The setting is a near-future megacity on a Hong Kong model where people have swapped more and more of the body for machinery and plug their brains straight into the network, which keeps the question of where a person stops and a machine starts permanently open. The Major, Motoko Kusanagi, is artificial from the neck down and human inside her skull, and she hunts the hacker known as the Puppet Master, who walks into other people's minds. The director of the film is Mamoru Oshii, who had made Patlabor before it.

Kusanagi is field commander of a small government counter-terror outfit under Chief Aramaki, with Batou as her second, and its name is among the most quoted designations in cyberpunk: Public Security Section 9.

The look of the thing changed the industry. For the famous fall from the skyscraper roof, and for the glowing data and the ghostly transparency, the studio put the traditional multi-plane camera together with a tool nobody had yet used this way in anime, which was computer graphics for compositing over hand-drawn cel animation. The Wachowskis showed the film to Joel Silver as the visual pitch for The Matrix, which is how much of the West met it second-hand.

rurouni-kenshin.context_blurb:
Rurouni Kenshin begins where the samurai story usually ends: the 1870s, the sword age finished, Japan rushing into trains and telegraphs. Nobuhiro Watsuki's wanderer carries a cross-shaped scar on his cheek and a past as the revolution's most feared killer, and he has sworn never to take another life. His katana makes that oath physical, because the sharpened edge sits on the inside of the curve and the blunt back faces the enemy. A reverse-bladed sword like that is a sakabato.

The Kyoto arc is the one everybody remembers. Kenshin goes back to the old capital to stop the assassin who took over his work when he walked away, a man the government tried to burn alive and who survived wrapped head to foot in bandages, now meaning to pull the young Meiji state down with a private army of killers: Makoto Shishio.

Keishi Otomo filmed the story in 2012 with Takeru Satoh, who had spent more than a year learning real sword-drawing technique, and the 2014 sequel finally took on the Kyoto story under the title Rurouni Kenshin: Kyoto Inferno. A second half followed later that year, and a two-part conclusion arrived in 2021.

The 1996 anime hit the trouble every long adaptation hits. Watsuki was still drawing one weekly chapter at a time, and Studio Deen ran clean out of book to adapt: the anime had caught up with the manga, so the studio invented an arc of its own. Fans have never thought much of it.

trigun.context_blurb:
Trigun is a Western in space. Yasuhiro Nightow's desert planet has two suns, almost no water, and frontier towns built by colonists whose ships crash-landed generations ago. Through them walks a tall, spiky-haired gunman in a red duster who insists he is a pacifist and who leaves wreckage behind him everywhere, which is why his bounty poster opens nearly every episode. The figure printed on it is sixty billion double dollars.

He carries a long silver revolver, but the arm holding it is the dangerous part. The prosthetic on his left side, a gift from his twin brother Knives, unfolds into an angel-arm energy cannon. Both brothers are Plants, grown from the same living technology that lights the colony's cities.

The comic came out twice over. Shonen Captain carried three volumes from 1995 and then folded, so Nightow moved the story in 1998 to the magazine Young King OURs, where fourteen more volumes ran under a new name: Trigun Maximum. Madhouse's 1998 anime adapts only those first three volumes and invents an ending of its own.

The whole look is a love letter to Sergio Leone. The stance, the coat, the twirl and above all the pistol were drawn from the gun Clint Eastwood carried through the Dollars trilogy, a converted Colt 1851 Navy.

slayers.context_blurb:
Slayers began as Hajime Kanzaka's comedy-fantasy novels in 1989 and reached television in 1995 through the studio J.C.Staff. Its heroine is a tiny, red-haired sorceress of about seventeen with an ego the size of the continent and a temper to match, and she makes her living by ambushing and robbing bandit gangs, which is why shopkeepers bolt their doors when Lina Inverse rides into town. The nickname the bandits and rival mages hang on her, the one that costs her her composure instantly, is Bandit Killer.

She travels with a dim blond swordsman, Gourry Gabriev, a chimera of a man stitched together out of several creatures, Zelgadis Greywords, and a crusading princess, Amelia Wil Tesla Saillune. The four of them argue their way through dragons, dark lords and very bad puns.

Towns flatten around her because of one spell. It is black magic that borrows a demon lord's own power, and it leaves a smoking crater where a village used to stand: the Dragon Slave. Megumi Hayashibara voiced Lina for a decade across television, films and radio dramas, which is much of why Slayers is still handed to anyone who loves fantasy adventures and has never watched anime.

lupin-iii.context_blurb:
Monkey Punch, whose real name was Kazuhiko Kato, began drawing Lupin III in 1967: a thief in a loud jacket and a skinny tie who steals impossible treasures and laughs while he does it. The surname is inherited. He is billed as the grandson of the gentleman burglar Maurice Leblanc began writing for Paris readers in 1905, Arsene Lupin. Leblanc's estate objected for years to the unlicensed grandson, which is why the character was renamed for several overseas releases.

The crew is fixed. Daisuke Jigen shoots, in a grey suit and a fedora; Goemon Ishikawa the thirteenth says almost nothing and cuts almost anything with his sword; and the fourth member sells the others out whenever the money is better, sometimes a partner, sometimes a rival, sometimes a lover, and her name is a joke about a mountain peak: Fujiko Mine. Hunting all four across the planet is a rumpled Japanese policeman seconded to Interpol, forever one step short of the arrest, Inspector Zenigata. Monkey Punch named him for Heiji Zenigata, a detective out of Edo-period fiction.

The film to start with is the 1979 feature, in which Lupin breaks into a pocket European duchy to get a young woman named Clarisse out of a forced marriage. It was the first cinema feature directed by the animator who went on to found Studio Ghibli, Hayao Miyazaki. His old mentor Yasuo Otsuka ran the animation overall, but the chase that made the film immortal, with the little yellow Fiat climbing a cliff face on momentum alone, was drawn by Miyazaki himself, key animation and all. Steven Spielberg is said to have called it the best action sequence he had seen in any medium.

Yasuo Yamada was the voice of Lupin for a generation. When he died in 1995 the part passed to the actor who has carried it through the television specials ever since, Kanichi Kurita. The fortieth-anniversary refresh in 2011 replaced nearly the whole original cast in one season and left him the only holdover.

The villain's title belongs to a real man. Giuseppe Balsamo, who styled himself Count Alessandro di Cagliostro, toured the courts of eighteenth-century Europe as a self-advertised alchemist and Freemason, selling diamonds and miracle elixirs that were frauds, and he was swept up in the 1785 Affair of the Diamond Necklace that helped topple the French monarchy. Miyazaki welded that swindler onto an invented principality of forgers.

osamu-tezuka.context_blurb:
Japanese comics were a children's novelty until one man turned them into a medium for stories. Born in 1928 and drawing all through the war as a boy, he handed the form its grammar: cinematic page layouts, huge shining eyes, plots that run for volumes. In 1952 he drew a robot built in the image of a scientist's dead son, with rockets in his feet, guns in his hips and lasers in his fingers, and Astro Boy made his name. The artist is Osamu Tezuka.

Cartooning was his second profession. Tezuka trained in medicine, qualifying as a physician at Osaka University with the degree and the licence in hand, and only then chose the drawing board over the clinic, which is why his surgeon-vigilante series Black Jack reads as though a doctor wrote it. He founded the Mushi Production studio in 1961, and in 1963 his robot boy became the first weekly half-hour animated series on Japanese television, which is where the whole industry starts.

One work he called his lifework. He began it in 1954 and was still drawing it when he died in 1989, never reaching the final volume he had planned: a story that leaps from ancient Japan to deep-space settlement, following an immortal firebird and the mortals who are born again and again around it, Hi no Tori, which English editions call Phoenix. Hayao Miyazaki, who thinks most of Tezuka's animation was rushed and cheap, has said it is the one manga he would most have liked to film.

sailor-moon.context_blurb:
A clumsy Tokyo schoolgirl called Usagi Tsukino, whose name means rabbit, is told by Luna, a black cat who talks, that she is the reborn princess of a lost kingdom on the moon. When she transforms she wears a sailor-suit uniform and a tiara, and her warrior name is Sailor Moon. Her friends change with her, one for each planet, and the enemies grow from street-level monsters to whole cosmic empires across five long story arcs.

The comic ran in Nakayoshi magazine from 1991 to 1997, and the woman who drew it reshaped the entire magical-girl genre: Naoko Takeuchi. Toei's 1992 anime carried the series around the world in dozens of languages, and the toy money made her one of the wealthiest manga authors in Japan.

The English version was less faithful. DIC cut about half a dozen episodes, renamed most of the cast, and quietly recoded the romance between Sailor Uranus and Sailor Neptune as nothing more than affection between cousins. Viz Media's 2014 redub restored the original characters and relationships, and the manga-faithful remake Sailor Moon Crystal arrived the same year.

my-hero-academia.context_blurb:
Kohei Horikoshi began My Hero Academia in Weekly Shonen Jump in 2014, in a world where nearly every child arrives with a power called a Quirk and the best of them go professional: licensed, ranked, paid and televised. The boy at the centre of it arrives with nothing at all. Other children twist the word for useless into a nickname for him, Deku, until a classmate hands it back as a hero name that sounds instead like an order to keep going.

The hero at the top of the rankings is a huge blond slab of a man whose grin works like public infrastructure: while people can see it, they are not afraid. He is All Might. In private he is the gaunt, hollow-cheeked Toshinori Yagi, and his power is the rare kind that can be handed on, gathering strength with each holder, which is why he chooses a powerless middle-schooler as his successor and gives him One For All. That power came out of a feud between two brothers at the dawn of Quirks: one could steal powers and stockpile them, while the other could hand a single power down the generations, and the pair of them sit at the centre of the entire story as All For One and One For All.

Class 1-A is built out of contrasts. The loud one sweats nitroglycerin out of his palms and sets it off, hates losing more than he fears dying, and spent his childhood tormenting the hero: Katsuki Bakugo. The quiet one freezes with the right half of his body and burns with the left, and wears a scald scar over one eye from the day his mother's mind gave way under his father's training regime; he is Shoto Todoroki. The father is the second-ranked hero Endeavor, who arranged a marriage for the ice Quirk in it, hoping to engineer a child who could beat All Might.

The villains answer to a young man whose skin is dry and cracked and whose touch crumbles whatever he holds. His master, the original thief of Quirks, is sealed in a prison underground. The leader is Tomura Shigaraki, born Tenko Shimura, grandson of the seventh holder of All Might's power and raised by that villain after his own Quirk killed his family.

The first fight the fandom calls a classic comes at the school's Sports Festival in the second season, where the ice-and-fire student meets the hero in a semi-final and loses to an argument rather than to a punch: bleeding and half-broken, Deku talks him into believing that the fire on his left side is his own and not his father's, and that is what makes him finally use it. The tournament itself goes to Bakugo, so furious at the way he won it that he has to be chained to the podium for the medal ceremony.

Class 1-A's homeroom teacher looks half asleep and is the most dangerous man in the building. Shota Aizawa, the underground hero Eraser Head, switches off another person's Quirk just by looking at him, and the kanji of his given name means to wipe out or extinguish, which is the joke buried in it: his own name points at an eraser. His eyelids are the limit, because the power stops the instant he blinks. Looped round his neck is his capture weapon, a long binding scarf woven of cloth over steel wire, which he throws, wraps and hauls with in the seconds when nothing is cancelled.

hajime-no-ippo.context_blurb:
Boxing comics usually open on a prodigy. This one opens on a bullied kid who smells of fish bait, hauling rope on his widowed mother's charter boat before school and getting shoved around in the corridors after it. A young professional pulls the bullies off him, walks him into a Tokyo gym, and the boy finds out that the one thing he is frighteningly good at is hitting people. His name is Ippo Makunouchi. George Morikawa began the comic in 1989 for Weekly Shonen Magazine and has never stopped drawing it.

The fighter who saved him is the gym's star, a hulking middleweight who shadow-boxes for an hour with one arm roped behind his back and who later takes title after title on his way up through the weight classes: Mamoru Takamura. The coach is Genji Kamogawa, a prizefighter in the lean years after the Second World War, who once rescued Takamura from life as a street thug and who refuses at first to hand Ippo the technique the boy wants most.

That technique is the Dempsey Roll, a weaving, rolling uppercut Ippo assembles out of slowed-down tape of an American champion, and it carries the name of Jack Dempsey, the heavyweight who held the world title from 1919 to 1926 by making himself a target that never stopped moving.

Ippo's most personal title fight puts him against an Osaka brawler nicknamed the Naniwa Tiger, a loudmouth who had already floored him once with a hook thrown from a crouch, the Smash, and who ends up the closest thing Ippo has to a true rival: Takeshi Sendo. Morikawa built him loosely on the real Japanese fighter Takenori Hosaka.

A long flashback drops into occupied Japan in the late 1940s. There an arrogant American officer, Ralph Anderson, leaves Kamogawa's friend Nekota brain-damaged with an illegal rabbit punch, and Kamogawa answers him with his fearsome, self-destroying Iron Fist.

The gym's off-season camps are what every sports comic since has copied. On the sand of a sleepy seaside town, Kamogawa sets Takamura to dragging a horse-drawn carriage tire behind him like a sled, hour after hour, up the dunes, until his legs stop arguing.

Morikawa took his research ringside, watching live bouts at halls such as Korakuen in Tokyo, and he went further than drawing gyms: he owns a real working boxing gym in Tokyo, JB Sports Gym. Long before that he had a famous assistant for a short while, a teenage Kentaro Miura, who went on to create Berserk.

demon-slayer.context_blurb:
Koyoharu Gotouge drew Demon Slayer in Weekly Shonen Jump from 2016 to 2020, and Ufotable in Tokyo turned it into one of the most watched anime ever made. The setting is Japan's Taisho era, around the 1910s: demons eat people after dark, and a secret order of swordsmen hunts them with black blades. A gentle charcoal-seller comes home to find his family killed and his little sister Nezuko the only one alive, half turned into a demon, so he joins the Demon Slayer Corps looking for a cure and carries her on his back in a wooden box. He is Tanjiro Kamado.

He picks up two companions. One is a jumpy blond who weeps and begs to go home and then, the instant terror knocks him out, moves in his sleep as a Thunder Breathing master of appalling speed, and he is Zenitsu Agatsuma. The other was raised in the mountains, wears a boar's head over his face and fights with two chipped blades, and he is Inosuke Hashibira.

Nine elite swordsmen called Hashira stand above the Corps, each with a Breathing Style. The one who spares Tanjiro and Nezuko in the very first chapter wears half a patterned haori, says almost nothing, and is the Water Hashira, Giyu Tomioka. The tall blind man with the prayer beads and the chained flail, reckoned the strongest of the serving pillars, is the Stone Hashira, Gyomei Himejima. Every one of these styles descends from an original invented by a Sengoku-era swordsman called Yoriichi Tsugikuni, which Tanjiro's family had preserved without knowing it as a religious dance: Sun Breathing (Hinokami Kagura).

The villain is the first demon ever made, past a thousand years old, undone by a single ray of sun, hiding in Tokyo as somebody's husband and father and making new demons by mixing his blood into human wounds. He is Muzan Kibutsuji. Twelve lieutenants called the Kizuki serve him in upper and lower ranks.

The 2020 film Mugen Train outgrossed every Japanese film ever made, passing a record Spirited Away had held for twenty years, and the Hashira it puts at the centre, aboard a haunted overnight train, is Kyojuro Rengoku, the Flame Hashira. The demon who kills him had been a martial artist named Hakuji before Muzan turned him, and he is Akaza, Upper Moon Three.

Part of why the fights look the way they do is technique. Ufotable blends drawn cels with carefully tuned computer work, and for Tanjiro's water attacks the studio used a custom CGI-and-2D blend called digital chiaroscuro shading, with hand-painted Japanese-watercolor overlays, first developed for its Fate adaptation in 2011.

The manga closed in May 2020 after a final fight of some eighty chapters. Muzan bites Tanjiro as he dies, turning him for a moment into the strongest demon there has ever been, and the one who gets through to him is his sister Nezuko, who reverses his demon transformation through her own restored humanity. She had won her own humanity back earlier with the help of Lady Tamayo's medicine. Gotouge then gave the cast a quiet epilogue a hundred years on, in modern Tokyo, where the reborn characters live ordinary lives, and the one drawn alone in a cafe with a book is Kanao Tsuyuri's reincarnation, reading a romance novel at a Tokyo cafe.

naruto.context_blurb:
Naruto ran in Weekly Shonen Jump for fifteen years, 1999 to 2014, all of it drawn by Masashi Kishimoto. The hero is an orphan in a bright orange jumpsuit with three whisker lines on each cheek and a bottomless appetite for ramen, held at arm's length by the adults of his village because a nine-tailed fox demon was sealed inside his belly in infancy. He wants the village's highest office, Hokage. He is Naruto Uzumaki.

Even the boy's name is a joke about his appetite: it comes from narutomaki, the swirled pink-and-white fish cake laid on a bowl of ramen, and his surname, Uzumaki, means a spiral or whirlpool. Kishimoto wanted a childish catchphrase for him, so Naruto tacks dattebayo onto his sentences, a meaningless brag that the first English dub turned into Believe it!

Home is the hidden village set deep inside the Land of Fire, behind an enormous wooden gate and beneath a cliff where the faces of all its past leaders are cut into the rock: Konohagakure, the village hidden in the leaves. Five great countries each keep one such village — Konoha, Kiri, Suna, Kumo and Iwa — and a Kage runs each of them.

Team 7's teacher is late to everything, keeps his left eye covered by a slanted headband, and reads in public a racy orange paperback written by the wandering sage Jiraiya. Behind the headband sits a Sharingan eye, which copies any technique it watches, and it is why the village calls him the Copy Ninja. He is Kakashi Hatake.

Jiraiya, a wandering sage and one of the three legendary ninja, teaches the boy to spin a ball of chakra in his open palm, a technique the Fourth Hokage had designed and left unfinished: the Rasengan. Naruto completes it years later by folding his wind nature into the sphere.

Kishimoto has a double in the business. His identical twin brother, Seishi, drew 666 Satan (O-Parts Hunter to English readers), and its art looked so much like Naruto's that some readers cried copying, though the two had simply drawn side by side since early childhood.

Shippuden takes the story up two and a half years on and brings in the Akatsuki, nine renegade ninja in black cloaks printed with red clouds. Their opening move is to carry off the red-haired desert ruler who had once been an enemy and is now among Naruto's dearest friends, Gaara, the Fifth Kazekage. He carries the one-tailed beast inside him.

The boy began as something else entirely: in Kishimoto's 1997 trial story for Akamaru Jump, the hero was a young fox spirit passing himself off as a human child, and a still earlier idea, never printed, would have made him a cook.

Kishimoto had nearly given up drawing in his early teens, until a promotional image for Katsuhiro Otomo's film Akira dazzled him into studying Otomo's art and copying the style. As a younger boy he had worshipped Akira Toriyama, and the cheek of Toriyama's Goku went into Naruto. Kishimoto did his homework on the sealing scrolls as well: the chants, the dragon ink and the ward patterns come out of Mikkyo, the esoteric Buddhism whose mountain centre is Mount Koya, braided together with Shinto rite.

one-piece.context_blurb:
Eiichiro Oda has been drawing One Piece for Weekly Shonen Jump since July 1997, and it is now the bestselling comic ever printed. Its captain, Luffy, is a cheerful idiot in a battered straw hat whose arms stretch and snap back like rubber, because as a small boy he ate one of the cursed fruits that hand out a power and take away the eater's ability to swim for good: a Devil Fruit. His was the Gum-Gum Fruit.

The hat is a loan: the red-haired pirate captain Shanks left it with the boy in Windmill Village, on the promise that Luffy would return it once he had grown into a great pirate. Shanks paid for that friendship with his left arm, lost saving Luffy from a monstrous sea beast called a Sea King.

What he is chasing is the hoard the last Pirate King left at the far end of the ocean road called the Grand Line, named after the dying king's own remark about leaving everything he had in one place: the One Piece. Roger was executed in public twenty-two years before the story opens, and the broadcast of his last words sent half the world to sea. That stampede is what the World Government calls the Great Pirate Era.

The crew assembles by trade: a cook, a sharpshooter who lies, a navigator, a reindeer doctor, an archaeologist, a cyborg shipwright, a skeleton musician. The first mate is a scowling swordsman with green hair and a black bandana who fights with three blades at once, one in each fist and the third clamped in his teeth, and he is Roronoa Zoro. His style is called Santoryu, and the white-sheathed sword he carries belonged to a childhood friend.

Devil Fruits sort into three families. Paramecia do odd things to a body, like Luffy's rubber; Zoan turn the eater into an animal; and the rarest and strongest family lets a man become an element itself, fire or magma or light or darkness, which is Logia. Willpower has a system of its own, Haki: one kind armours a blow, one kind senses what the eye cannot, and the third turns up in about one person in a million, cannot be trained but only woken, and drops weaker men unconscious when its holder simply exerts it. That one is Conqueror's Haki.

Oda traces his love of pirates to a cartoon from his early childhood, Vicky the Viking, about a quick-witted little Viking boy, because it showed him that Vikings are really pirates of a sort. Akira Toriyama's Dragon Ball shaped his drawing more than anything else. He served his apprenticeship helping other artists, and by nineteen he was working on Nobuhiro Watsuki's samurai hit Rurouni Kenshin, where Watsuki credits him with helping to create the character Honjo Kamatari.

Underneath it all lies the Void Century, a hundred-year hole in the record roughly eight centuries back, when nineteen kingdoms, whose descendants run the World Government today, wiped out a civilisation whose name has been suppressed ever since and survives only as the Great Kingdom. When Oda pitched all this to his editor in 1997 he thought it would run about five years and some two hundred and fifty chapters; he went past eleven hundred chapters long ago.

bleach.context_blurb:
For fifteen years from 2001, Tite Kubo drew Bleach for Weekly Shonen Jump, and it made its name on sword designs, long coats and villains with nicknames. An orange-haired high-school boy has always been able to see ghosts. One night a small Soul Reaper called Rukia Kuchiki comes through his bedroom wall chasing a soul-eating monster, is wounded, and passes her powers to him so that he can protect his family, and the boy is Ichigo Kurosaki. The huge cleaver he ends up carrying is a zanpakuto named Zangetsu, and a Soul Reaper's zanpakuto is sealed until its owner speaks its name and its release command.

Those swords nearly never existed: Kubo first imagined Soul Reapers armed with guns, which is why the project's early name was Snipe, and only late in development did the firearms become blades. He tried Black and White as titles before settling on Bleach, and when Jump turned down the first proposal, Akira Toriyama, the creator of Dragon Ball, wrote Kubo a letter of encouragement.

Behind the living world is the Soul Society, an afterlife built like feudal Japan and guarded by thirteen squads, the Gotei 13, each with a captain. At the start of the story the captain-commander is a scarred old man with a long beard who had founded the whole organisation a thousand years before, Genryusai Shigekuni Yamamoto. His walking cane is not a cane. Toshiro Hitsugaya, the youngest captain the Gotei has ever had, releases an ice dragon with the words reign over the frozen heavens, and the squad he leads is Squad 10.

The arc most readers rate highest is the third and longest, in which Ichigo and his friends break into the Soul Society to reach a condemned comrade before her execution, climbing at last to the tower where she is held: Senzaikyu, the Tower of Penitence atop Sokyoku Hill. It runs about sixty chapters and more than forty episodes, and it ends on one of the best cliffhangers in the series.

The manga ran to 686 chapters, ending in August 2016 with an arc called the Thousand-Year Blood War. Studio Pierrot animated that last arc in three runs between 2022 and 2024, nearly a decade after the comic finished, which is a rare second chance for an anime and worth watching on that account alone.

attack-on-titan.context_blurb:
Hajime Isayama drew Attack on Titan from September 2009 to April 2021, and the premise is a nightmare a child grasps at once: the last of humanity lives inside three rings of enormous stone wall, because outside them walk naked giants that eat people. The outer wall is Maria and the middle one Rose, and the innermost ring, where the king and the capital sit in safety, is named Sina. When something colossal kicks the outer wall open the giants come through, and three young friends enlist, ending up in the Survey Corps, the unit that goes outside.

The comic nearly landed somewhere else: Isayama first showed his pages to Shueisha's Weekly Shonen Jump, whose editors wanted his style reworked for their magazine, and he said no. He carried the story to Kodansha instead, and it ran in the monthly Bessatsu Shonen Magazine.

The Survey Corps' gear is why the action looks like nothing else: an Omni-Directional Mobility rig that fires grapples into a tree or a titan's shoulder and swings the soldier through the air. The badge on their green jackets, one white wing crossed over one blue, got the nickname Wings of Freedom, and Isayama has said he took it from a real unit, the British Royal Air Force's Pathfinder squadron of WWII, whose job of finding targets in the dark matches what the Corps does. The ranks, the boots and the European names come out of the same research.

The anime arrived in 2013, and the first three seasons, the ones people remember for the sky-diving combat, were animated by Wit Studio. MAPPA took the final season from 2020, after Wit turned down the heavy computer work the later titans needed.

The Survey Corps' most famous soldier is its short, scowling captain, Levi. Isayama built Levi on the vigilante Rorschach from Watchmen, whose film he had seen, then made him fanatically clean as a joke on Rorschach's filth.

Isayama grew up in Oyama, a corner of Hita in Oita Prefecture closed in by mountains, and in front of Oyama Dam there now stand child-sized bronzes of the three friends, Eren, Armin and Mikasa, staring up at the concrete as if it were Wall Maria. Fans paid for them, Isayama advised on them, and his handprint and signature sit beside them. The manga ended in 2021 at 139 chapters.

death-note.context_blurb:
Tsugumi Ohba wrote Death Note and Takeshi Obata drew it, in Weekly Shonen Jump between 2003 and 2006, and Madhouse animated it from 2006. A black leather notebook falls out of the sky in Tokyo because a bored death god called Ryuk wants to see what a human will do with it. Anyone whose name is written inside dies, provided the writer can picture the face, and the brilliant, bored schoolboy who picks it up and starts killing criminals with it is Light Yagami. He takes a nickname that is the English word killer run through Japanese sounds, and the press and the police end up calling him Kira.

The police cannot explain a world of dying criminals, so they call in a detective who works through an intermediary, sits crouched on his heels, lives on cake and sweets and will not give a name, going by a single letter: L. He is three top detectives rolled into one identity, and the name itself is a weapon against him, since anyone holding a Death Note could kill him by writing it, which is why almost nobody knows that he is L Lawliet. He was raised at Watari's orphanage, Wammy's House.

The first meeting face to face is a trap on both sides. Light and L are named joint top scorer at an entrance ceremony and introduce themselves under false names, L borrowing the name of a real Japanese pop singer as a private joke, and the place is To-Oh University, fictional Tokyo Imperial-style elite institution. Earlier, in a sequence famous for running both men's inner monologue at once over close-ups of a ball and a racket, each watches the other for a tell: the activity is a televised tennis match Light watches while L watches him watching. In chapter 58 Light works out that he is under close surveillance, lists six lettered contingencies in his head from A to F, and the one he runs is Plan B, the contingency that involved a specific date-marked notebook-page. What he thinks to himself afterwards became one of the most quoted lines in anime.

L does not last the whole story. Two orphans from Wammy's House divide his role between them, one white-haired and fond of marshmallows, the other blond and fond of chocolate, and their names are Near and Mello. Near, whose real name is Nate River, works on the floor among his toys and dice, and the tic Obata drew over and over is that he twists a single lock of his white hair around his index finger.

The book itself was copied from a real object. Obata redrew the cover several times and worked from a prop the publisher's team made for him, a Moleskine-style notebook with custom hand-cut leather cover provided by Shueisha's production team, grain and stitching and page edges and all. If you like a thriller in which almost nothing happens except two people thinking at each other, this is the one everybody recommends first.

fullmetal-alchemist.context_blurb:
Hiromu Arakawa drew Fullmetal Alchemist from 2001 to 2010, and there are two anime: the 2003 one, which overtook the comic and invented an ending, and the 2009 Brotherhood from Studio Bones, which follows her to the last page. The world runs on alchemy, a science of rearranging matter through drawn circles, bound by a law of equivalent exchange in which nothing comes from nothing.

Two brothers break the deepest taboo of that law in an attempt to raise their dead mother. The rebound takes an arm and a leg from the elder and the whole body of the younger, whose soul his brother pins to a hollow suit of armour with a blood seal, and who stops to rescue stray cats wherever he goes; he is Alphonse Elric. The state certifies the elder at twelve, the youngest State Alchemist there has ever been, with a silver pocket watch and the title that names the series: The Fullmetal Alchemist. What the two of them met in the instant the ritual failed was the Gate of Truth, with the entity called Truth at its threshold, which collects the toll in person. It is also why Edward can transmute by clapping his hands instead of drawing a circle: he had seen the Gate of Truth and 'paid the toll' for human transmutation knowledge.

The country the brothers live in is drawn as early-1900s Germany with alchemy where the gunpowder should be, and it is called Amestris. Its state alchemists are soldiers, officially human weapons. The man in the blue uniform who snaps his ignition-cloth gloves to burn an enemy to ash, and who means to climb to the top and pull the regime down from the inside, is Colonel Roy Mustang. He fought in the Ishvalan campaign and has never got over it.

Against them stand seven artificial people named for the deadly sins, made by an ancient homunculus called Father, who intends to swallow every soul in the country at once. The first of them the brothers run into is a tall woman, dark-haired, with a red mark on her chest, and the sin she carries is Lust. Father's design required the nation's wars to be arranged in advance and the army steered from the top, and the Fuhrer who did the steering, himself a homunculus with an eye that reads any opponent's next move, is King Bradley.

Brotherhood ran through five opening themes, and the first of them, the fast rock song called Again, belongs to Yui (a solo artist, not a band), whose 'Again' opens Brotherhood's first arc. Arakawa grew up on a Hokkaido farm and put more theology, and more about war guilt, into a boys' adventure comic than anyone expected it to carry.

hunter-x-hunter.context_blurb:
Hunter x Hunter is Yoshihiro Togashi's second great comic, running in Weekly Shonen Jump since 1998, and its subject is a licence. A Hunter's card opens locked archives, funds expeditions and buys silence, which is why the examination that grants it kills most of the people who sit it. The boy chasing one is twelve, spiky-haired, raised by his aunt on Whale Island, and hunting the father who left him as a baby: Gon Freecss. Ging Freecss, it turns out, is one of the strongest Hunters alive.

The examination is a gauntlet — a marathon through poisoned marsh, a wild animal cooked to the standard of a fussy judge, a knockout tournament aboard an airship. The tiny, wizened old man who sets those trials and chairs the licensing association is Isaac Netero.

Gon's best friend is a runaway, the twelve-year-old heir of the most feared family of assassins in the world, whose estate on Kukuroo Mountain is shut behind doors graded by tonnage. Something is chained at the outer gate, and it is not a trap and not a Nen beast. It is a dog the size of a small house, trained to recognise the family bloodline and to tear apart anybody who does not carry it, and his name is flatly, comically ordinary: Mike.

With the exam behind them, Gon and that friend, Killua, fight their way up a skyscraper of a stadium called Heavens Arena, bout by bout and floor by floor, and there Wing, a mild-mannered teacher, opens their eyes to Nen. Nen is a life-energy that every user shapes in exactly one of six ways. A personality test sorts them: a drop of water floats above a glass and the aura does something to it, and what it does tells the examiner which kind of fighter the student is. Gon's kind is the bluntest of the six, pure Enhancement, which pours aura into his own body and his own fist so that he can go straight through whatever stands in front of him.

Togashi draws in bursts, because his spine will not let him do anything else. The longest silence ran from November 2018 to October 2022, and through it he posted page counts on Twitter like a man filing reports from a sickbed; four years of work came to roughly ninety-five pages, released as ten chapters that made up a single volume of the Dark Continent expedition. He married into the trade, too: his wife, Naoko Takeuchi, the creator of Sailor Moon, had helped shade the single-color pages of the very first Hunter x Hunter volume with screentone before the two wed in January 1999.

jojos-bizarre-adventure.context_blurb:
Hirohiko Araki has been drawing the same family since 1987: nine numbered Parts, each in a new decade and a new country, each starring a Joestar whose name folds down to the two syllables JoJo. Victorian England, then wartime Europe, then Egypt, then a quiet Japanese town, then Naples. The muscles are enormous, the poses come straight off a fashion runway, and almost every fight is won by working out a rule rather than by hitting harder.

Part 3, Stardust Crusaders, is where most readers start. A Japanese delinquent in 1988 finds a star-shaped mark on his neck and discovers that he can call up a violet fighting spirit, which he names Star Platinum; with his grandfather Joseph Joestar he has fifty days to cross the world to Egypt and save his dying mother. He is Jotaro Kujo. Those ghost-fighters, humanoid guardians made of willpower that nobody without one can even see, were given the name the whole series now runs on: Stands. The first two Parts had used a breathing art called Hamon instead. Araki modelled him on Clint Eastwood, down to the pointing pose, borrowed from Eastwood with a .44 Magnum, and the grumbled yare yare daze, Japanese for good grief, which mimics the kind of line Eastwood growled on screen.

Waiting in Egypt, hidden in a mansion, is the vampire Dio Brando, more than a hundred years old. His Stand stops time, and the English dub's shout for it, Za Warudo, escaped into internet culture. Every Stand in that arc is named for a card of the tarot's Major Arcana — Star Platinum for the Star, Magician's Red for the Magician, and Dio's own for the twenty-first card, the World — while from Part 4 onward Araki names them after the rock records he loves, which is why the anime studio has to rename or blur a few of them for streaming.

Part 4 trades the world tour for a single seaside town, Morioh, where a high schooler named Josuke Higashikata keeps finding Stand users next door. Araki drew Morioh from the place he knew best, his own hometown of Sendai in Miyagi Prefecture, where a big JoJo exhibition opened in 2012. Morioh also gave him the character he later sent to Paris: when the Louvre asked five artists for comics that take place within its walls, for a 2009 exhibition, Araki's story starred Rohan Kishibe, the town's touchy comic-book artist, whose Stand can open a person up like a book and read him.

Part 5 crosses to Italy in 2001 behind a mafia recruit of fifteen, Giorno Giovanna. His Stand, Gold Experience, breathes life into whatever its fists strike, and like the Stands after Part 3 it wears a record's name: Prince had put out an album called The Gold Experience in September 1995, a few months before the Part began.

Araki names two sources for the look himself. Italian Renaissance painting is why his figures twist like marble statues, and Italian high-fashion photography from the 1960s through the 1980s, above all the Versace campaigns, is where the clothes and the impossible stances come from.
