yu-yu-hakusho.context_blurb:
Yu Yu Hakusho means Ghost Files. Yoshihiro Togashi drew it for Weekly Shonen Jump between 1990 and 1994, and it opens with its hero dying: a middle-school delinquent with a slicked-back pompadour shoves a small boy clear of a speeding car and takes the hit himself. The afterlife is so surprised by the gesture that it offers him a second life as a Spirit Detective. He is Yusuke Urameshi.

Togashi, a fan of the occult and of horror films, first showed his editors the drafts as How to be a Ghost. He then wanted to call the series YuYu-Ki, until another manga with a sound-alike name, Chin-Yu-Ki, got into print first, so he tacked on Hakusho, report, the first word that occurred to him.

Yusuke's weapon is his own hand: he cocks his index finger like a gun barrel and fires a blast of spirit energy from its tip, the Spirit Gun, or Rei Gun, a trick he learns with help from Botan, the Spirit World's ferry girl.

The tournament is the stretch everyone remembers, a multi-day knockout contest on an island, staged by demon gangs with money on the outcome, running thirty-five episodes of the anime. It is the Dark Tournament.

Studio Pierrot turned the comic into a hit TV anime in 1992, and its cheerful opening song, Matsuko Mawatari's 1992 single Hohoemi no Bakudan, takes its name from the Japanese for Smile Bomb. The weekly schedule wore Togashi down, and he brought the manga to an end in 1994 with its final arc badly cut short.

initial-d.context_blurb:
Initial D is about a boy who does not know he is a driver. Shuichi Shigeno began it in Young Magazine in 1995 and ended it in 2013: a quiet Gunma high-schooler carries tofu down a mountain road in the dark in his father's ancient Toyota, and has been trained without noticing since the age of thirteen by an order never to spill the cup of water sitting on the dashboard. He is Takumi Fujiwara. His father Bunta, a touge legend in his own right, never bothered to explain.

The car matters as much as the driver. A Trueno AE86 in panda paint, white over black, had already been out of production for ten years when the comic started, and its chassis code gave the fans the nickname everybody still uses: Hachi-Roku, which is simply eight-six said in Japanese. Toyota built the GT86 in 2012 because that nickname refused to die.

Every road in the story is a real one. Akina, the downhill Takumi owns, is drawn from Mount Haruna in Gunma, and the other courses keep their own names — Myogi, Akagi, Usui, Irohazaka — so readers could drive the comic, and did. By the late nineties real drift drivers treated the passes as pilgrimage.

The sound is Italian. Avex Trax packaged the fast, thumping dance music into one long-running album line, Super Eurobeat, until it was as recognisable as the artwork. The label's house star, with more placements than anyone across the early episodes, recorded as Dave Rodgers, born Giancarlo Pasquini, and his 'Deja Vu' and 'Speedy Speed Boy' are what a generation hears in its head when a car tips into a downhill corner.

Project D is the touring team Takumi joins alongside Keisuke Takahashi for the long final arc, and the comic closes in July 2013 on a deliberately untidy, bittersweet finish against a younger driver built as Takumi's mirror, Shinji Inui. The venue is home ground, Mount Akagi. Shigeno's world carries on in MF Ghost, where Takumi is the elder statesman.

toilet-bound-hanako-kun.context_blurb:
Kamome Academy has seven ghost stories that students whisper to each other, and at this school every one of them turns out to be a real spirit with its own territory and its own rules. As a set they are called the Seven Mysteries. The seventh is a boy who haunts a third-floor stall in the old girls' lavatory.

A shy, superstitious first-year summons him to ask for a love potion, finds herself bound into his service instead, and sprouts fish scales on her legs whenever her feelings run high, which ties her to the school's Mermaid Mystery. She is Nene Yashiro. The ghost she calls Hanako-kun had a human name of his own, and it was Amane Yugi.

A loud red-haired boy out of a long family line of exorcists joins them, training to banish exactly the sort of spirit he has just befriended: Kou Minamoto. His older brother is the strongest exorcist in the school.

The third mystery is a back staircase where climbing to the top trades one person's soul for another's, and the spirit in it is a girl named Misaki, bullied into taking her own life on those stairs decades earlier.

The Mokke, tiny fox spirits shaped like lumps of mochi, run errands between the Mysteries, and the coin they trade in is a star-shaped sugar sweet the Portuguese brought to Japan in the sixteenth century: konpeito.

Hanako and his twin Tsukasa both died at thirteen, and Amane killed his brother before dying himself, which is the question the manga keeps circling. The twins played the violin and grew up in an ordinary working family's neighbourhood, with a seamstress mother who was often out of the house.

Lerche animated the 2020 series in soft pastel watercolours with chalk-on-blackboard transitions, so that nothing in it ever quite looks frightening. The opening theme, credited to an invented group put together out of the voice cast, is called No.7.

anime-misc-classics.context_blurb:
This one is a shelf rather than a single series: eleven Japanese classics worth hunting down, each with a fandom of its own.

Kazuki Takahashi's 1996 manga puts a shy boy called Yugi Mutou in a place called Domino City, where the game shop belongs to his grandfather Sugoroku, and an ancient Egyptian puzzle turns him into a champion of a card game full of dragons and wizards; the series is Yu-Gi-Oh! Konami launched the real trading-card game off the back of it in 1999, which is why those cards exist at all.

Rumiko Takahashi is among the best-selling comics authors who ever lived, and two of hers are on the shelf. Her first big hit, which ran from 1978 to 1987, starred Lum, a horned alien princess in a tiger-stripe bikini who flew through the air and electrocuted her human fiance Ataru whenever he misbehaved, and its punning title is Urusei Yatsura. The later one drops a schoolgirl named Kagome down a dry shrine well five hundred years into the past, where she meets a silver-haired boy with dog ears who carries an enormous sword and hunts the shards of a broken jewel with her, and that series is Inuyasha.

Yoichi Takahashi began Captain Tsubasa in 1981, about a boy named Tsubasa Ozora who means to play for Japan in a world cup, and the sport is soccer. Lionel Messi, Zinedine Zidane, Andres Iniesta and Fernando Torres have all said the comic shaped them as children, which may be the largest real-world footprint any manga has.

Buronson wrote and Tetsuo Hara drew Fist of the North Star in 1983, set in a nuclear wasteland, where a seven-scarred master of a Chinese-style killing art strikes hidden pressure points and walks away before his enemies burst, and the warrior is Kenshiro. His line about an opponent already being dead is among the most quoted in anime.

Sunrise's Code Geass arrived in 2006. An exiled Britannian prince hiding as a Tokyo schoolboy takes a mind-control power from an immortal green-haired girl called C.C. and raises a masked rebellion against his own family, and the prince is Lelouch. The mask carries a name of its own, and leading the Black Knights against the occupation, his alter ego is Zero.

Gainax made six episodes of FLCL in 2000, the ones people pronounce Fooly Cooly, which open with a pink-haired alien roaring into a sleepy town on a yellow Vespa and clouting a bored twelve-year-old called Naota with a blue electric bass, and she is Haruko. The Pillows did the soundtrack and it outlived the show.

Shinichiro Watanabe followed Cowboy Bebop with Samurai Champloo in 2004, scored in hip-hop by Nujabes, in which a waitress named Fuu gets two rival swordsmen, feral Mugen and stoic Jin, to walk Edo-period Japan with her while she looks for a samurai from her childhood, identified by one odd detail, which is that he smells of sunflowers.

Yuki Urushibara's Mushishi, animated in 2005, is the quiet one. A white-haired traveller called Ginko walks old rural Japan with a wooden medicine chest, treating people harmed by half-visible primal creatures that are neither plant nor animal and that most people cannot see, and the show calls them mushi. They gather around Ginko wherever he goes, which puts everyone near him at risk, and his defence is a habit: he smokes constantly to suppress the mushi he naturally attracts.

Takehiko Inoue drew Slam Dunk between 1990 and 1996, in which a red-haired troublemaker in his first year, Hanamichi Sakuragi, joins the basketball team in Kanagawa to impress a classmate, and his school is Shohoku. Inoue storyboarded and directed the 2022 animated film himself. Akira Toriyama's gag comic Dr. Slump and Bandai's Digimon round out the shelf.

princess-bride.context_blurb:
The Princess Bride is a bedtime story with a frame round it: a grandfather, played by Peter Falk, reads a book to a sick boy who keeps interrupting to complain about the kissing. Rob Reiner directed it in 1987 from a novel of 1973, and the writer who produced both the book and the screenplay, a rare double, is William Goldman, the screenwriter whose verdict on Hollywood was that nobody knows anything. He had already won Oscars for Butch Cassidy and for All the President's Men.

On the farm where the story opens, the hired boy answers every single request the farm girl makes of him with the same three quiet words, and by the time she works out that they mean he loves her, he has gone to sea. The three words are as you wish.

Buttercup is carried off by three men: a Spanish fencer, a giant, and a bald, bellowing Sicilian who is certain he is the cleverest creature alive. Each time a plan collapses, or the masked climber behind them declines to fall off the Cliffs of Insanity, Vizzini throws the same long word at the problem as though the word itself could repair it: inconceivable. The fencer tells him, politely, that he does not think it means what he thinks it means.

The hero and Buttercup cross the Fire Swamp, which offers three ways to die: sand that swallows, flame that bursts out of the ground, and enormous rats whose existence the hero flatly denies about four seconds before one of them bites him. Fans shortened their name, rodents of unusual size, into ROUSes. The rats were stuntmen in suits, and some of them really were set carefully alight.

The fencer and the giant carry their friend, mostly dead but not quite, up to a miracle man the prince once sacked: Miracle Max, Billy Crystal under an hour of latex, who sells them a chocolate-coated pill. His wife, played by Carol Kane, leans out of the doorway as the three set off and wishes them a good time storming the castle. Crystal and Kane improvised much of what people still quote.

Fezzik, the giant with the gentle voice, is Andre the Giant, the French wrestler billed at seven feet four. His size came of a pituitary disorder that kept his body making growth hormone long past childhood, acromegaly, and it was what finally wore his heart out, in 1993, at forty-six. He arrived straight from the most famous match of his life, against Hulk Hogan at WrestleMania III in April 1987 in front of ninety-three thousand people, and he arrived hurt: surgeons had just been at his back, so his scenes were rigged with hidden supports that took his weight whenever Fezzik lifts somebody. Mandy Patinkin, who plays the fencer, read his lines aloud to him, because Andre was dyslexic. Three years earlier Andre had played the horned brute in Conan the Destroyer.

Reiner's own first film, three years before this one, was a mock documentary following a doomed American tour by a British heavy-metal band whose amplifiers go up to eleven: This Is Spinal Tap. The cliff-top duel between the fencer and the man in black was performed almost entirely by Cary Elwes and Patinkin themselves, trained by Bob Anderson, a British Olympic fencer of 1952 who spent decades quietly choreographing film swordplay, most famously for Star Wars, where he wore Darth Vader's costume for the lightsaber duels while David Prowse wore it elsewhere.

The boy in the bed is Fred Savage, eleven years old and already cast in the television series that would run six seasons from January 1988, The Wonder Years. The game on the Commodore Amiga 1000 beside him was chosen by the production designer Norman Reynolds, who had designed Star Wars and The Empire Strikes Back. It is Accolade's first hit, programmed by Bob Whitehead and published in 1985: Hardball!, and not the 1989 sequel Hardball II that half the internet names, which did not yet exist when this film was shot.

Goldman's novel pretends to be his own abridgement of a far longer classic by an invented author called S. Morgenstern. Readers who wrote in asking for the unabridged text were promised the one scene he had supposedly cut, the reunion between Westley and Buttercup, and then received a polite form letter from the publisher explaining that the Morgenstern estate would not permit it to be reprinted. The estate did not exist either.

back-to-the-future.context_blurb:
Back to the Future came out in 1985, directed by Robert Zemeckis, written with Bob Gale and produced by Steven Spielberg's Amblin. A California teenager gets thrown back to 1955, interrupts the night his parents met, and has to repair his own family history before he fades out of a Polaroid. The machine that takes him there is a stainless-steel car with gull-wing doors, a DeLorean DMC-12, picked because Zemeckis wanted something that would look like a spaceship to 1955 eyes. It needs 88 miles an hour and a flux capacitor.

Doc Brown, played by Christopher Lloyd, greets every impossibility in all three films by grabbing his white hair and shouting two old-fashioned words: Great Scott! He says it in 1955, in 1985, in the 2015 of the second film and in the 1885 of the third.

The casting nearly went another way. Zemeckis shot four or five weeks with a serious young actor in the lead, then decided he was too dramatic for a comedy, and that actor was Eric Stoltz. Amblin paid him in full and reshot almost everything. The actor who took over the part was Michael J. Fox. He was tied to the sitcom Family Ties, so he filmed at night and at weekends for months, sleeping in his car between sets.

The jokes are built to pay off. Marty lands in 1955 in a red puffer vest of a kind nobody there has ever seen, and the locals decide it is a life preserver (they think he's a sailor who fell off a boat). Reading his underwear label, they start calling him Calvin Klein. In the diner he asks for a Tab, which was Coca-Cola's diet brand, and then for a Pepsi Free, and the gag is that Tab and Pepsi Free, both soft drinks of 1985, mean nothing at all to a soda clerk in 1955, who tells him he cannot have a tab unless he orders something.

The locations and the stunts were real. The mall where the DeLorean makes its first jump is Puente Hills Mall in Industry, California (despite often being misidentified as Burbank), and the Twin Pines turning into Lone Pine on Marty's return is one of the film's small payoffs. The clock tower stands on the Universal backlot, on a courthouse set built in 1962 for To Kill a Mockingbird, and the cable-swinging climax looks lethal because of a trick: the cable was attached to Lloyd's stunt double via a hidden harness, and a pulley counterweight system did most of the swing motion.

The second film, in 1989, guessed at 21 October 2015 and filled it with hoverboards, self-lacing Nikes and a nineteenth Jaws sequel on a cinema hoarding. One guess landed, and it startled Bob Gale when it did: the Cubs winning the World Series in 2016 (just one year late from the film's October 21, 2015 prediction), ending the longest drought in American sport. Start with the 1985 film; the other two only make sense after it.

ghostbusters.context_blurb:
Ghostbusters came out in 1984, directed by Ivan Reitman and written by two of its stars, Dan Aykroyd and Harold Ramis. Three parapsychologists lose their university posts and open a commercial ghost-removal business in a disused Manhattan firehouse, with proton packs and traps of their own making, and a fourth man joins them for wages. The job ends on a rooftop against a Sumerian god who demands that they name the form of their own destructor, at which point Ray thinks of the most harmless thing he knows and a hundred-foot mascot in a sailor hat comes up Fifth Avenue: The Stay-Puft Marshmallow Man.

Aykroyd wrote the script with three friends in mind for the parts, one of them John Belushi, who died in March 1982 before a frame was shot. Bill Murray took the part of Peter Venkman and played it, Aykroyd has said, as a tribute to the energy Belushi had brought to Animal House (1978) and The Blues Brothers (1980) — Belushi's Bluto/Jake energy translated into Venkman. Eddie Murphy, also in the original plan, had Beverly Hills Cop to make, and the part written for him became Winston Zeddemore, played by Ernie Hudson.

The marshmallow man was a man in a suit. The stuntman Bill Bryan wore it on a tabletop New York, shot to make him look a hundred feet tall, and the effects were run by the man behind Poltergeist and Return of the Jedi, Richard Edlund and his Boss Film Studios. That sequence cost more than every other effect in the film put together.

Ray Parker Jr's theme spent three weeks at the top of the Billboard chart and then went to court, because Huey Lewis sued for similarity to 'I Want a New Drug' (1984); the case settled out of court. The settlement carried a confidentiality clause that Lewis later broke in an interview, and he was sued over that in turn.

The 1989 sequel sends a river of pink slime under Manhattan, fed by bad temper, and its villain is a sixteenth-century Carpathian tyrant living inside his own portrait, played by a German former professional boxer who acted under the name Wilhelm von Homburg (real name Norbert Grupe). Reitman had Max von Sydow dub the lines. The climax turns the Statue of Liberty into a weapon, and the trick is that the team plays 'Higher and Higher' by Jackie Wilson to charge the slime with positive emotions.

The Saturday-morning cartoon began in 1986 under J. Michael Straczynski, who later made Babylon 5 and who did not want the green ghost Slimer promoted to a regular. ABC insisted, the ratings agreed, and from 1988 the show was called Slimer! and the Real Ghostbusters. Straczynski quit that year.

scott-pilgrim.context_blurb:
Bryan Lee O'Malley drew Scott Pilgrim as six small black-and-white paperbacks between 2004 and 2010, and Edgar Wright filmed it in 2010 with Michael Cera. Books and film share one snowy setting, the Canadian city he was living in through his twenties: Toronto. Even the money is local, because the eight dollars Scott hands over at the cinema was what a ticket there actually cost in 2010, a detail American audiences took for a joke about his wallet.

Scott is twenty-three, broke, and plays bass in a garage band with Stephen Stills and the drummer Kim Pine. The band is named after a Mario enemy: Sex Bob-omb. Their songs for the film were written by Beck, with Nigel Godrich overseeing the music. Scott cannot afford a flat of his own, so he sleeps in the bed of a roommate who is gay, far cleverer than he is, and walks off with every good line: Wallace Wells.

When he meets the American delivery girl with the changing hair, he is still going out with a starry-eyed Catholic schoolgirl of seventeen who thinks he is the coolest man alive, and whom he drops without ceremony: Knives Chau. Ramona Flowers was played on screen by Mary Elizabeth Winstead, with Anna Kendrick as Scott's sister and Aubrey Plaza as the foul-mouthed Julie. To date Ramona properly he has to beat each of her former partners in video-game combat, and the number of evil exes is seven.

In the books you can tell which volume you are holding by Ramona's head, because the dye job changes with every one: pink first, then blue, then green. Her fourth ex is the only woman he has to fight, a katana-carrying girl out of Ramona's college days: Roxie Richter.

The third ex, Todd Ingram, draws his strength from being vegan, and the Vegan Police come for him the moment he cheats, first over the half-and-half he stirs into his coffee and then over a chicken parmigiana. Beating him earns Scott a sword, which arrives with an item screen in the style of an old role-playing game, and the tag on it reads plus two against evil ex-boyfriends.

The last fight belongs to Gideon Graves, who runs a record label. The film stages it in a club modelled on Lee's Palace on Bloor Street, but in the comics the venue is Gideon's own concert hall, the Chaos Theatre. Scott wins with a second blade, the Power of Self-Respect, which he can only draw after facing Nega-Scott, the part of himself carrying the memories he will not own: how badly he treated Knives Chau and Envy Adams.

Edgar Wright bought the rights in 2005, before the second book had even reached the shops, and the film took that book's title: Scott Pilgrim vs. the World. The casting turned out to be a forecast of the decade, since Brandon Routh had already played Superman and Chris Evans went on to play Captain America. The film lost money on release and then found its audience on video, and a Netflix anime in 2023 brought the original cast back to voice the whole comic.

super-mario-bros-movie-2023.context_blurb:
Illumination and Nintendo made The Super Mario Bros. Movie in 2023, and it took more than a billion dollars. It opens on two Italian-American plumber brothers who have just started a business of their own and live with a loud extended family in one borough of New York: Brooklyn. A sewer job drops them down a warp pipe into the Mushroom Kingdom.

Princess Peach, raising an army against Bowser, sends Mario through an obstacle run of saw blades and fireballs to find out whether he is any use. Her voice belongs to Anya Taylor-Joy. Jack Black's Bowser sits at a grand piano aboard his airship and sings her a love ballad that became a radio hit in its own right: Peaches. The song was shortlisted for an Academy Award. Aaron Horvath and Michael Jelenic directed the picture, Seth Rogen voices Donkey Kong, and the Penguin King who defends the Snow Kingdom is Khary Payton, for years the voice of Cyborg on Teen Titans. The rest of the score, arranging the old Nintendo game themes throughout, was written by Brian Tyler.

The film is stuffed with Easter eggs. The brothers' own television advertisement, animated to look like a worn videotape, recreates a Nintendo promotional tape from 1989, the era of the second Mario game. Donkey Kong's grumpy father, Cranky Kong, is no new invention: he is the original Donkey Kong of the 1981 arcade cabinet, the one where Jumpman climbed girders after a woman named Pauline. In the kart chase along Rainbow Road, the item that homes in on whoever is leading and knocks Mario clean off the track is the Blue Shell.

The Snow Kingdom is a tour of Super Mario 64. Its cabin and its slide come from Cool, Cool Mountain, the peak with the lost baby penguin on it, while Bowser rolling huge snowballs across the ice at the penguins repeats Chief Chilly's attack in Snowman's Land.

terminator-franchise.context_blurb:
James Cameron wrote The Terminator in the early 1980s and then refused to let go of it. The producers wanted a director with a record behind him, so he let the whole script go for a single dollar on condition that he direct it himself. The film cost six and a half million and took seventy-eight.

Arnold Schwarzenegger was nearly cast as the human soldier rather than the machine. The switch happened over lunch, and nothing on the table had anything to do with it: Cameron simply worked out that the bulk and the accent belonged to the cyborg. At a Los Angeles police desk the cyborg is told he cannot come in, answers "I'll be back", and minutes later drives a car through the front doors.

The 1991 sequel makes Arnold's old model the bodyguard and sends something worse after the boy, a cyborg of liquid metal that pours through bars and grows blades out of its arms: the T-1000. Cameron's first pick for that part was the rock singer Billy Idol, until a motorcycle crash left Idol with a badly injured leg. The role went instead to Robert Patrick, an unknown whose home at the time was his car, and the casting director Mali Finn saw in him exactly the intensity the part needed.

Industrial Light and Magic wrote custom morphing software for the T-1000, the work of an engineer who later took an Academy Award for the technique, Doug Smythe. Michael Jackson's Black or White video copied the effect within months.

The boy at the centre of it all was a complete unknown too. Mali Finn found him as well: Edward Furlong, thirteen years old and hanging about with friends at a YMCA in Pasadena, with no acting experience at all.

karate-kid.context_blurb:
The Karate Kid, in 1984, set the shape every underdog sports film has borrowed since. Daniel LaRusso moves from New Jersey to a stucco apartment block in Reseda, California, with his widowed mother, gets beaten up by boys from a local dojo called Cobra Kai, and is quietly taken in hand by the building's handyman, an old Japanese-American gardener called Miyagi, who teaches karate by making the boy wax cars and paint fences until the motions live in his arms.

It comes down to the All-Valley tournament final, one leg hurt and the other holding him up. Daniel opens his arms wide, like a bird about to take off, and kicks from his one good leg, using the move he had watched Miyagi practise on the sand: the crane kick.

The director already knew the shape, because he had built it once before. John Avildsen had won the directing Oscar in 1977 for a film about a broke Philadelphia club fighter handed one shot at the heavyweight champion, Rocky. Pat Morita's Miyagi earned a Best Supporting Actor nomination of its own.

Even the title was borrowed: DC Comics already owned a Karate Kid, a martial artist created in 1966 for its Legion of Super-Heroes, and in 1984 the filmmakers got DC's permission to use the name for the film and its sequels.

Pat Morita knew the war years first-hand. Born in Isleton, California in 1932, he spent nine years in a Sacramento hospital with spinal tuberculosis, and was then interned with his family at Gila River in Arizona before a security reclassification moved him to Tule Lake in California. He came out of the camps into restaurant kitchens, then stand-up comedy, then Happy Days, then the part that defined him.

top-gun.context_blurb:
Top Gun cost fifteen million dollars in 1986 and took three hundred and fifty-seven, which turned Tom Cruise into an action star. Tony Scott, Ridley's younger brother, directed it. The young Navy aviator who reports to the fighter-weapons school at Miramar, flies the F-14 and breaks every rule in the manual has a call sign that fits him: Maverick.

The jets were real, so the Navy had a say. It read the script and asked for changes: the opening dogfight left Cuba for international waters, and a crash on a carrier deck was cut. Charlie, Maverick's love interest, was first written as an enlisted sailor, and because officers may not date enlisted personnel the Navy had her turned into a civilian contractor. The Navy got a recruiting boom out of the film.

Real ships came with real bills: when a carrier changed course mid-shot and spoiled Scott's light, he was told that swinging the ship back would cost $25,000, so he paid it with a check made out to the captain and carried on filming. The black MiG-28s the hero fights were really American Northrop F-5s in disguise.

One sequence never reached the screen at all. Cruise came close to drowning during an ejection-seat drill shot underwater in the pool at Miramar, and the producers cut it on liability grounds. His later habit of doing his own stunts starts about there.

The beach volleyball scene was Don Simpson's late addition, made over Scott's objections, and it set the shirtless-action-hero image Cruise then carried through the next decade of his films.

Nine years later Scott set Gene Hackman and Denzel Washington at each other's throats over a missile launch aboard a submarine: Crimson Tide.

the-goonies.context_blurb:
The Goonies, in 1985, came from a Spielberg story, a Chris Columbus script and Richard Donner's direction, the same Donner who had already made The Omen and Superman. A gang of middle-school friends in Astoria, Oregon, about to lose their houses to a golf-course developer, find a three-hundred-year-old treasure map in an attic and follow it into the caves under their town.

The crooks squatting in the derelict restaurant over those caves are a hard Italian-American crime family: Mama, two sons called Jake and Francis, and a brother they keep chained in the cellar. They are the Fratellis. That chained brother is huge, gentle and disfigured, and once the children cut him loose he shares a Baby Ruth with Chunk and never leaves his side. He is called Sloth. John Matuszak, a former professional footballer, played him under hours of make-up.

Mikey was Sean Astin, years before Samwise Gamgee, and his mother had been a film star herself, an Oscar winner at sixteen who had played Helen Keller as a girl: Patty Duke. Josh Brolin was seventeen on set.

Cyndi Lauper wrote and sang the theme. Two years earlier her first solo album had thrown off four top-five singles and sold six million copies: She's So Unusual.

Chunk was Jeff Cohen, who does the belly-shaking truffle shuffle on the doorstep. He quit acting as a teenager, went through law school at UCLA, and now works as an entertainment lawyer representing studios and talent.

Two pieces of lore sit outside the story. One-Eyed Willy was nobody in particular, an invention of Chris Columbus rather than a real buccaneer, and the full-size pirate ship built for the climax was never destroyed: Donner refused to break it up, so it sat in a warehouse for years before being scrapped in the early 2000s. The cut scene with the one-eyed octopus, the one Data still mentions in the finished film, survives in the television edit and as a bonus feature on the 2010 Blu-ray.

et-the-extra-terrestrial.context_blurb:
Steven Spielberg's E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial opened in 1982, written by Melissa Mathison, with Henry Thomas as Elliott and a seven-year-old Drew Barrymore as his sister. A three-foot alien is left behind by his own ship in a California suburb and hides in a tool shed, and the boy coaxes him indoors with a trail of sweets up the stairs. Mars turned down the chance to use M&Ms, Hershey paid a million dollars instead, and the candy on the lawn is Reese's Pieces. It is the most cited product placement in the history of the movies, because sales tripled, making it one of the most successful product placements in film history.

The video game is the other half of the legend. Atari paid upwards of twenty million dollars for the licence, ordered five million cartridges, and gave the whole job to one in-house programmer with about five weeks to deliver before Christmas, and that programmer was Howard Scott Warshaw. He had designed Yars' Revenge the same year and still defends the game. Only a third of the cartridges sold. Trucks hauled the rest into a desert landfill and buried them under concrete, and the city was Alamogordo. Everybody treated that as an urban legend until a documentary crew dug the site up in April 2014 and found the cartridges exactly where the story said they were.

indiana-jones.context_blurb:
Harrison Ford's archaeologist teaches undergraduates in a tweed jacket and robs tombs in a leather one. George Lucas and Steven Spielberg built him in 1981 as a deliberate throwback to the Saturday-matinee serials of their own childhoods, where the hero outran a trap every fifteen minutes, and they handed him a bullwhip and a soft felt hat with a dented crown and a snapped brim: a fedora. The standing order on set was that the hat never gets lost.

Raiders of the Lost Ark drops him into 1936, racing Hitler's agents for the gilded chest the Israelites carried out of the desert with the stone tablets Moses brought down from Sinai inside it, a relic the Führer believes will make his armies invincible: the Ark of the Covenant. Those same jackbooted enemies return eight years later for the third film, which is why the honest answer to whom Indy spends the trilogy punching is the Nazis. Spielberg liked them for a simple reason: no audience objects to watching a Nazi get hit.

The first five minutes of Raiders are the whole series in miniature. Deep in a Peruvian temple Indy reaches for a small gold figure standing on a pressure-plated pedestal and slides a bag of sand onto the stone as he lifts the idol away. He guesses the weight wrong, which is why a boulder the size of a bus comes down the corridor after him.

The 1984 film is a darker prequel, pitting him against a Thuggee death-cult in India with a Shanghai street kid riding shotgun. Short Round was played by a boy born in Saigon who also turned up as Data in The Goonies, walked away from acting in the nineties to coordinate stunts, and came back to win an Academy Award in 2023 for Everything Everywhere All at Once: Ke Huy Quan.

The Last Crusade, in 1989, explains the man by introducing his father, a medieval historian who has chased the Holy Grail since before his son could walk. The casting is the joke, because Indy's dad is Sean Connery. Spielberg wanted the family tree literal: the adventurer had been modelled on a spy in the first place, so he hired the actor who had played James Bond through the 1960s and let the audience do the arithmetic. Connery was twelve years older than Ford, which is to say barely old enough for the job.

The hunt ends in front of a wall of cups guarded by an immortal knight. When the greedy financier drinks from the gaudiest goblet, which is the wrong one, the knight's verdict runs to three dry words: he chose poorly.

Lucasfilm hid its own history in these films. The Jones pictures trade Star Wars jokes from the start: C-3PO and R2-D2 are cut into the hieroglyphs of the Well of Souls in Raiders, and the Shanghai nightclub where the second film opens is Club Obi-Wan. The Grail temple's rose-coloured face is a real tomb front at Petra in Jordan, cut from the cliff some twenty centuries back by the Nabataeans, and its Arabic name, Al-Khazneh, means the Treasury, because local Bedouins believed riches lay inside the carved urn high on its front. They shot at the urn to break it open, but it is solid sandstone. Thirty seconds of Petra reach the screen, and it is the shot nobody forgets.

schwarzenegger-80s-action.context_blurb:
Set the Terminator films aside and Arnold Schwarzenegger still owns the decade, mostly through three pictures.

John Milius filmed Conan the Barbarian in 1982, with the Cimmerian hunting the snake-cult sorcerer who killed his parents. Thulsa Doom was played by the deepest voice in American cinema, the one that also spoke for Darth Vader: James Earl Jones. The line on screen before anything happens, about what does not kill us making us stronger, is genuine Nietzsche, out of Twilight of the Idols in 1888. The riddle of steel, by contrast, is Milius's own invention. The music came from a Greek-American composer who also scored RoboCop and The Hunt for Red October: Basil Poledouris. Milius asked for Wagner as a Mongol horseman might have written it, and the opening piece, Anvil of Crom, rests on a choir singing over hammers beating real anvils, with timpani and brass underneath. Poledouris hired blacksmiths to do the beating.

Predator, in 1987, drops a special-forces team into a Central American jungle to be hunted one man at a time. John McTiernan directed it in the middle of the best three-year run any action director has had, because after it came Die Hard in 1988 and The Hunt for Red October in 1990. When the helicopter at last drops in among the trees, Dutch roars at the survivors to get to the chopper.

The first alien suit was a spindly insect thing with a long red neck, worn for a day or two by Jean-Claude Van Damme, and the star and the director hated it so much that the redesign went to the creature sculptor behind Aliens and The Thing: Stan Winston. The man inside the new suit stood seven feet two and played the friendly Bigfoot Harry the same year: Kevin Peter Hall. The heat-vision shots are no optical trick either, because the crew filmed them on a real industrial thermal camera, an Inframetrics 525 of the sort used to hunt roof leaks. The mud Dutch cakes himself in to hide from that camera came out of McTiernan's reading on jungle warfare, where Vietnam veterans were said to have used mud against enemy night optics.

Total Recall, in 1990, gives us a construction worker who might really be a Mars spy whose memory was wiped. Philip K. Dick wrote the 1966 story it came from, We Can Remember It for You Wholesale. David Cronenberg held the project for a while in the early 1980s and walked away from it over arguments with the producers. Paul Verhoeven took it instead and loaded it with exploding heads and Martian mutants, among them the three-breasted dancer in the bar, played by an actress who left the business for working journalism, Lycia Naff. The ratings board sent the film back eight times before granting an R, and the scene it kept balking at is the subway shootout, where Schwarzenegger holds a dead body in front of himself and lets the bullets go into it.

alien-franchise.context_blurb:
Alien began in 1979 with Ridley Scott's film about the crew of a deep-space towing ship, the Nostromo, who answer a distress call and bring something aboard. It was sold on one of the great taglines, which promised that in space nobody would hear you scream. The creature came from a Swiss surrealist painter whom Scott hired after seeing his airbrushed art book Necronomicon, and the painter was Hans Ruedi Giger, who signed his work with his initials. Giger's biomechanical style, skeleton fused with machine, set the look of everything that followed, and it won him an Oscar.

James Cameron's sequel in 1986 changed the genre without changing the universe, turning a haunted-house picture into a war picture. The warrant officer from the first film wakes after decades of frozen sleep and goes back to LV-426 with a squad of Colonial Marines, and the character Sigourney Weaver played across four of these films is Ellen Ripley. The colony they reach is empty except for one child who has been living in the air ducts, and her family had named her Rebecca, but her brother called her Newt (real name Rebecca Jorden) because she could fit into all the small places. Carrie Henn, who played her, never made another film.

The hardware was real, which is why it still looks right. Stan Winston's team built the Alien Queen as a costume that stood fourteen feet, operated by two puppeteers inside and a crane for movement, with a rod-and-puppet crew of a dozen more off camera. Weaver, after a few rehearsals, insisted on driving the yellow power loader herself. Jonesy the cat was played by four trained cats.

Shooting at Pinewood went badly at first. Cameron wanted the pace he was used to in America, the British crew was used to another, and the story that gets retold is that he sacked the lot of them on day one. What happened is less cinematic: Cameron actually held his ground until the crew, expecting to be fired, came back, and the film was made. It cost about eighteen million dollars, drew seven Oscar nominations, won two, and earned Weaver a Best Actress nomination, which nobody expects for a film with xenomorphs in it.

Everyone assumed he would go straight on to a third. He did not, because Cameron's next film was The Abyss (1989), not an Aliens sequel, and the 1992 third film went instead to a young David Fincher. The 1979 original and the 1986 sequel are the pair to watch, in that order, on the same night if you can take it.

star-wars-original-trilogy.context_blurb:
George Lucas's three films, in 1977, 1980 and 1983, set a farmboy against an empire that can blow up planets. Luke grows up with an uncle and aunt on a moisture farm under two suns, among Jawas and sand people, on a world called Tatooine. Lucas took the name from Tataouine in southern Tunisia, where he shot those scenes.

The plot starts because Leia hides the Empire's most closely guarded secret inside an astromech droid and drops him onto that planet: the plans for the Death Star. The readout shows the exhaust port Luke flies down at the end.

Lucas wanted brass and strings instead of the synthesizers everyone else was using, so John Williams wrote a Wagnerian score of character themes and recorded it in England, at Denham, with the London Symphony Orchestra. One famous theme is missing from the first film, because Vader walks on to the main title in 1977 and the Imperial March only arrives with The Empire Strikes Back in 1980.

The Hoth walkers were animated a frame at a time by a man who blurred each frame with motion-control rods to kill the stop-motion judder, a trick he called go-motion, and who went on to supervise the dinosaurs of Jurassic Park: Phil Tippett. When Spielberg switched to computers, Tippett said he thought he had just gone extinct.

Wicket, the Ewok scout who finds Leia in the forest on Endor, was played by a boy of two feet eleven inches in his first film role, Warwick Davis, and he was eleven years old. He only got the part because Kenny Baker fell ill.

Mel Brooks spoofed the lot in 1987. Barf the Mawg, half man and half dog, floppy ears and bottomless appetite, was played by John Candy.

tombstone-wyatt-earp.context_blurb:
Tombstone, made in 1993, dramatises what really happened in an Arizona silver town in 1881. Kurt Russell plays Wyatt Earp, Val Kilmer plays the dying dentist and gambler Doc Holliday, and the red-sashed cattle rustlers they fall out with call themselves the Cowboys. Half a minute of shooting in a vacant lot behind a livery stable on 26 October left three of those men dead and made the Earps legends: the Gunfight at the O.K. Corral. It did not take place inside the corral at all, but in the lot behind it.

The three who died were Tom McLaury, Frank McLaury and Billy Clanton, while the man who had spent the previous night drunkenly promising to kill the Earps ran for his life unarmed once the shooting started: Ike Clanton. The gang's real ringleader, who shoots Fred White, the town marshal, while deep in an opium haze early in the film, was an outlaw called Curly Bill Brocius.

Holliday had trained properly for his first profession. He took a dental degree in Philadelphia in 1872, caught tuberculosis, and was ordered west for dry air, so he hung out his first shingle in a booming Texas cattle town: Dallas. Patients would not let a man who coughed blood work on their teeth, so he turned to cards. He never did die in a gunfight either, because tuberculosis took him in bed on 8 November 1887, aged thirty-six, in a Colorado mountain town the whole West knew for its hot mineral water: Glenwood Springs. In the film he faces down Johnny Ringo over an old Latin proverb, in vino veritas, meaning that there is truth in wine.

Wyatt Earp lived another half-century, drifting from one gold rush and gambling hall to the next and ending up in California. In 1920s Los Angeles he fell in with the silent-Western star Tom Mix and with a young prop boy at Fox who grew up to become John Wayne, and who said later that he had taken some of his walk from the old lawman. Earp died in 1929, and Mix and William S. Hart were at the funeral.

Most of what everybody knows about him came out of one book. Stuart Lake's biography of 1931 invented, among much else, the long-barrelled revolver the dime novelist Ned Buntline supposedly gave him; no record from the period mentions any such gun, and historians read the Buntline Special as Lake's own fiction.

The film's production was chaos. The screenwriter was handed the director's chair and then fired three weeks into shooting, and his name was Kevin Jarre, who had also written Glory. George Cosmatos replaced him on paper, and Kurt Russell has said for years that he did the real directing himself; in 2018 Cosmatos's son Panos confirmed it, describing his father as a paid frontman.

blade-runner.context_blurb:
Blade Runner opened in June 1982, directed by Ridley Scott and taken loosely from a 1968 novel by Philip K. Dick. Rick Deckard, played by Harrison Ford, is a worn-out ex-policeman in a Los Angeles of rain and neon whose job is to hunt manufactured people the Tyrell Corporation builds for labour in the off-world colonies, and the film's name for them is Replicants. Four of them have come back to Earth illegally.

Dick's novel carries one of the great titles, asking whether androids dream of electric sheep, and it is set in a world where the real animals have nearly gone and people keep electric pets to feel less alone. Almost none of that survives into the film, which borrowed its own name from an unrelated book, and the film the novel became is Blade Runner. Hampton Fancher wrote the first screenplay and David Peoples rewrote it. Dick saw twenty minutes of a rough cut late in 1981, was moved by it, and died of a stroke in March 1982, three months before the opening.

The sound of the film is one enormous keyboard. Vangelis, who had an Oscar in hand for Chariots of Fire, built nearly every cue on a rare Japanese synthesizer weighing something like two hundred pounds, and the instrument is The Yamaha CS-80.

The most quoted speech in science-fiction cinema came from neither screenwriter. Rutger Hauer, playing the replicant Roy Batty, cut the scripted lines right down and added the image of moments vanishing like tears in rain, and he did that writing the night before shooting, in his hotel room. The crew is said to have applauded the take. The fullest account of how it happened is in Future Noir, the definitive making-of book, whose author is Paul Sammon.

The release itself was a mess. Test audiences in Denver and in Dallas turned hostile in May 1982, confused by the pacing and the absence of narration, so Warner Bros. made Scott add a Harrison Ford voiceover, which Ford is reported to have delivered flatly on purpose in the hope that it would be dropped. The studio also tacked on a 'happy ending' featuring outtake footage from Stanley Kubrick's The Shining, aerial shots over forest that Kubrick had never used. The 1992 Director's Cut and the 2007 Final Cut removed both. Find the Final Cut: almost everything cyberpunk looks the way it looks because of this film.

don-bluth.context_blurb:
Don Bluth joined Walt Disney Animation in 1955 as a teenage in-betweener on Sleeping Beauty, rose to lead animator on The Rescuers, and walked out on 13 September 1979 with a dozen or more senior artists behind him. His grievance was craft: Disney was using xerography to cheapen the animation process and cutting fluid hand-drawn detail. Hand inking had gone, and so had the depth of the old multi-plane shots. The film the team abandoned mid-production was The Fox and the Hound (released 1981).

His own studio's first feature came in 1982, a grim fantasy in which a widowed field mouse looks for help for a sick child before the farmer's plough reaches her home, and it is The Secret of NIMH. Those letters stand for a real government laboratory. It follows a 1971 Newbery Medal novel about rats made clever by experiments, Mrs Frisby and the Rats of NIMH, whose author was Robert C. O'Brien. Bluth changed Frisby to Brisby to keep clear of a flying-disc trademark.

In 1983 he drew an arcade game. Cinematronics shipped a cabinet that played hand-drawn cartoon off a laserdisc while the player jabbed the joystick or the sword button on cue to steer a clumsy knight called Dirk the Daring past dragons, collapsing floors and spike traps, and the game is Dragon's Lair. The man who drew it, whose Disney pedigree is why it looked like a feature film, is Don Bluth. The woman Dirk is trying to reach is Princess Daphne. His team worked seven months and drew approximately 50,000 cels — three times the count of a typical 80-minute Disney feature, since a branching game must animate scenes most players never see. It took fifty cents a play against the usual quarter and queues formed anyway, yet arcade owners still lost money, because the laserdiscs wore out after roughly 10,000 plays and machines required constant repair. Sega published the follow-up in 1984, a space opera on the same technology, called Space Ace. Forty years on, it is the cabinet Dustin covets in Stranger Things, where the player logged as MADMAX takes his high score and turns out to be Maxine 'Max' Mayfield.

Steven Spielberg's Amblin then backed two Bluth features. The 1986 one follows a young mouse separated from his family on the crossing to America in the 1880s, and it is An American Tail (1986), about Russian-Jewish mice immigrating to America. The flight is historical, since the family is running from the Russian pogroms of the 1881-1884 period, which displaced over 2 million Eastern European Jews. Fievel is named for Spielberg's own grandfather, whose surname was Posner. The hit song, a duet across the New York night sky that reached the Billboard top five, got its depth the old way, from a multi-plane camera, the same technology Bluth had championed at Disney before his 1979 defection.

The 1988 one sends a young dinosaur called Littlefoot across a dying landscape after his mother's death, and the child who spoke every one of his lines was no star but Gabriel Damon, a 12-year-old child actor. Test screenings with children went so badly that Universal, with Spielberg and George Lucas, cut approximately 12 minutes, including a more graphic Sharptooth (T-Rex) attack and a longer death sequence for Littlefoot's mother. What was released runs sixty-nine minutes.

In 1989 Bluth made a hand-drawn musical set in the New Orleans of the 1930s about a German Shepherd gangster called Charlie B. Barkin, voiced by Burt Reynolds, and it is All Dogs Go to Heaven. Reynolds took the part for a private reason: his pet Doberman 'Bruno' had recently died, and the part connected him to processing the loss. It opened on 17 November 1989 against Disney's The Little Mermaid and was flattened.

One Disney picture of that decade gets blamed on Bluth and had nothing to do with him. The 1985 adaptation of Lloyd Alexander's Prydain books, with its undead army and its Horned King, was the first Disney cartoon feature to be rated above G, and the film that broke the streak was The Black Cauldron itself, in 1985. Bluth had been gone six years.

westerns-and-old-west-lore.context_blurb:
The Western started with real people and then invented itself on top of them.

The biggest cowboy star in film history was born in Winterset, Iowa in 1907 and christened Marion Robert Morrison, a name Hollywood would not have, so from 1930 he worked as John Wayne. John Ford cast him in 1939, over studio objections, as the Ringo Kid in a picture about nine passengers crossing Apache country, shot in Monument Valley: Stagecoach. Seventeen years later Ford handed him Ethan Edwards, a soured veteran of the Confederate army who spends year after year hunting the niece a Comanche raiding party carried off, in the film many critics still call the finest Western ever made, The Searchers. It was photographed by Winton Hoch, and the framed doorway that opens and closes it has been copied ever since. The novel behind it grew out of a real abduction, that of a nine-year-old Texan girl taken in 1836 who married a Comanche war chief, bore three children and lived twenty-four years with the band before Texas Rangers hauled her back in 1860: Cynthia Ann Parker.

Italy rebuilt the genre in the 1960s. Sergio Leone's three Dollars films put a squinting American in a poncho with a cigar in his teeth, the Man with No Name, and the actor was Clint Eastwood. The three-way standoff in the cemetery at the end of the 1966 film plays under a Morricone piece titled Il Triello, while the track just before it, as Tuco hunts for the grave, is L'Estasi dell'Oro. The 1968 epic opens on three gunmen waiting at a station while a fly crawls over one of them for minutes together, Leone's salute to the waiting-for-the-train tension of High Noon. He directed one further Western himself, in 1971, casting Rod Steiger as a bandit from Mexico and, as an Irish bomb-maker in the revolution, James Coburn: Duck, You Sucker.

Hollywood had already borrowed from Japan. The Magnificent Seven of 1960 is a remake of Akira Kurosawa's 1954 film about masterless samurai hired by farmers, Seven Samurai. Elmer Bernstein wrote its theme in two days, and from 1965 an advertising campaign carried it off for Marlboro cigarettes and Marlboro Country.

Eastwood kept the genre breathing. In Pale Rider, in 1985, he plays a preacher named out of Revelation, chapter six, verse eight, where the rider on the pale horse is Death. In Unforgiven, in 1992, he played an old killer taking one last job, and the supporting-actor Oscar went to the brutal sheriff Little Bill Daggett, played by Gene Hackman.

The real West sits behind all of it. Wild Bill Hickok was shot from behind, through the head, in a Deadwood saloon on 2 August 1876 holding two black aces and two black eights, which is why the dead man's hand is aces and eights. Jesse James was killed on 3 April 1882 in St Joseph, standing on a chair to straighten a picture, by a gang member who had been promised a pardon and a reward: Robert Ford. Billy the Kid, shot dead by Pat Garrett at Fort Sumner in July 1881 at the age of twenty-one, went by William H. Bonney as an adult but appears in his early records as Henry McCarty. Butch Cassidy rode with the Sundance Kid in a gang named for the red-rock hideout they wintered in, the Hole in the Wall in Wyoming's Big Horn Mountains. Doc Holliday, who had always expected a bullet, died of tuberculosis in bed at Glenwood Springs in November 1887; he looked down at his bare feet and remarked that this was funny.

Buffalo Bill Cody took his Wild West show on the road for thirty years from 1883 with real cowboys, real Indians, and a sharpshooter who could split a playing card edge-on at thirty paces: Annie Oakley.

Kevin Costner's Dances with Wolves took seven Academy Awards in 1990 and had its cast speak real Lakota on screen, coached by a language instructor from Sinte Gleska University, Doris Leader Charge. She taught Costner his verbs in her own female forms, so his lieutenant speaks Lakota like a woman from beginning to end.

saturday-morning-cartoons.context_blurb:
Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles began as a 1984 black-and-white parody comic from Kevin Eastman and Peter Laird. The orange mask and the nunchucks belong to Michelangelo, the purple mask and the bo staff to Donatello. Their food, invented for the cartoon, is pizza. April O'Neil reports for Channel 6 News. Her yellow jumpsuit was borrowed from Fujiko Mine of Lupin III. The 1990 live-action film, with Henson animatronics, was scored by John Du Prez.

Thundercats put cat-warriors on a ruined world they call Third Earth, led by the lion with the Sword of Omens, Lion-O. Their mummified enemy calls himself Mumm-Ra the Ever-Living, and the four Ancient Spirits of Evil were modelled on Egyptian, Greek, Norse and Aztec gods.

The Autobot leader who becomes a red-and-blue semi truck is Optimus Prime. His toy mould had been Takara's Battle Convoy. His rival Megatron folds into a Walther P38 handgun. Marvel's Bob Budiansky named the whole roster in one weekend, including Optimus Prime and Megatron. Orson Welles voiced Unicron in his last week alive, taking the job because he needed the money.

The Joe team's battle cry is Yo Joe. Prince Adam raises his sword and shouts by the power of Grayskull. Skeletor plots from Snake Mountain. Filmation reused one clip in nearly every episode, Prince Adam's transformation. The studio kept its animation in California because Lou Scheimer insisted. His twin sister, after her own Grayskull oath, becomes She-Ra. In The Problem with Power, Skeletor tricks He-Man into thinking he has killed someone.

Five lion machines combine into Voltron. Rankin/Bass sent part-metal heroes against Mon*Star as the SilverHawks. BraveStarr's talking, shooting horse is Thirty/Thirty. The marshal himself borrows a hawk's eyes, a wolf's ears, a bear's strength and a puma's speed. The masked leader driving the Thunder Hawk is Matt Trakker. The Centurions called their gear down by shouting Power-Xtreme.

Inspector Gadget's unseen villain, stroking his cat, is Dr Claw. The niece who really solves the cases is Penny. Gadget's voice was Maxwell Smart's own, Don Adams. The lasagne-eating tabby from Jim Davis's strip is Garfield. Porky Pig closed the Looney Tunes with three words: that's all folks. Mel Blanc lay in a coma until a doctor asked how Bugs Bunny was feeling, and he answered in character.

DuckTales opens with a two-syllable cheer, woo-oo. Scrooge was voiced throughout by Alan Young. The duck comics behind the show were drawn in secret by Carl Barks, who only admitted his authorship publicly in 1971. Darkwing Duck announced himself as the terror that flaps in the night. TaleSpin made a cargo pilot of the bear Baloo. The purple leader of Disney's stone gargoyles is Goliath. Its three immortal Weird Sisters come out of Macbeth, whose real seventeen-year reign is thought to have been peaceful and prosperous.

Tiny Toon Adventures was executive-produced by Steven Spielberg. The three Warner siblings are Yakko, Wakko and Dot. Yakko's World runs through every country to the Mexican Hat Dance. The Presidents runs through all forty-one to Rossini's William Tell Overture. The third voice cutting into I'm Cute is Dot, telling the boys she is cute. The Brain's grand voice is mostly Orson Welles: Maurice LaMarche practised on Welles's famous frozen-peas commercial outtake. Freakazoid turned into a comedy when Tom Ruegger took it over from Bruce Timm. Batman: The Animated Series was run by Timm with Paul Dini, who created Harley Quinn. Mark Hamill built his Joker laugh from the Wicked Witch and Claude Rains. Heart of Ice remade Mr Freeze as Victor Fries, trying to save his dying wife Nora when a lab accident left him needing cold to live.

The bald telepath at the mutant school is Professor X. The 1992 theme was composed by Ron Wasserman. The 1994 Spider-Man series was plotted almost single-handed by John Semper Jr.

Rugrats came from the studio of Arlene Klasky and Gabor Csupo, Klasky Csupo. Spike the dog was first meant to narrate and translate the babies. Ren and Stimpy's creator, fired in 1992, is John Kricfalusi. The episode held off the air for years is Man's Best Friend. Disney's Doug added a baby sister, Cleopatra, called Dirtbike. Hey Arnold came from Craig Bartlett. Recess's brainy girl with the hand-held computer is Gretchen Grundler. Captain Planet's five rings are earth, fire, wind, water and heart. The heart ring let Ma-Ti talk to animals and read feelings. Gi, who holds water, is from Asia. Captain Planet was voiced for all 113 episodes by David Coburn.

christmas-and-holiday-specials.context_blurb:
A Charlie Brown Christmas went out on CBS on 9 December 1965, and the network hated it in advance for being slow and sad, with no laugh track, real children's voices, jazz and scripture. Charlie Brown is sent for a tree, walks past the aluminium ones and brings back a scrawny little pine sapling. The jazz piano trio belongs to Vince Guaraldi, who wrote Linus and Lucy and scored the Peanuts films until 1976. Linus recites Luke 2 to explain what Christmas is about, and in the middle of it he drops his blanket at the line 'Fear not'. Schulz had insisted on the reading. The ratings answered them, because it got the second-highest Nielsen rating of the entire week, with 45 percent of all American TVs, and CBS ran it each December until 2019.

The stop-motion ones came from one small outfit. Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer arrived in December 1964, and the studio behind it, and behind Frosty too, is Rankin/Bass. The 1970 Rankin/Bass hour about how Santa first came to town gives grey Sombertown a pompous mayor who outlaws toys, and he is Burgermeister Meisterburger. The 1974 one about a year with no Santa sets the Heat Miser and the Snow Miser singing at each other until their mother settles it, and she is Mother Nature. How the Grinch Stole Christmas! came out as a rhyming picture book in 1957 and as a Chuck Jones half-hour in 1966 narrated by Boris Karloff, and the pen name on it was Dr. Seuss.

A Christmas Story, 1983, puts Ralphie Parker in 1940s Indiana wanting one present while every adult warns that he will shoot his eye out, and what he wants is A Red Ryder BB gun. His father wins a Major Award, a lamp shaped like a leg in a fishnet stocking, and reads what is stamped on the crate aloud as though it were a word: FRAGILE — and the father reads it as 'fra-GEE-lay, must be Italian'. The prop was built for the film in Cleveland, and at a 2014 auction the original fetched Over $100,000 — to a private collector.

National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation, 1989, hands a suburban father a disastrous holiday and a bonus envelope holding A one-year membership in the Jelly of the Month Club. The actor playing Clark Griswold, for the third time in the series, is Chevy Chase.

Home Alone, 1990, strands an eight-year-old when his family flies to Paris, and the boy who defends the house with paint cans and glue is Kevin McCallister. John Hughes wrote it, and the director, who later made the first two Harry Potter films, is Chris Columbus. The gangster movie Kevin plays to scare off the pizza boy is a fake, shot in one day for Home Alone: Angels with Filthy Souls. The house is real: 671 Lincoln Avenue, Winnetka, Illinois, where fans still turn up.

Elf, 2003, sends Will Ferrell out of the North Pole in yellow tights, and its director, who launched Iron Man in 2008, is Jon Favreau.

The Nightmare Before Christmas belongs to both holidays. It began as a three-page poem Tim Burton wrote at Disney in 1982, and it was a Dr. Seuss-style rhyming poem, much shorter and not yet sung. Burton designed and produced the 1993 film but was busy with Batman Returns, so the three years of frame-by-frame animation were run by Henry Selick. Chris Sarandon spoke Jack Skellington; the singing voice, and all ten songs, came from Danny Elfman. Disney thought the thing too dark for its own name and put it out through Touchstone Pictures.

The Polar Express, 2004, is Robert Zemeckis's motion-capture version of Chris Van Allsburg's 1985 book, and Tom Hanks performed six separate roles in it, the conductor and Santa among them. The child has no name in the book and none in the film either, where he is credited as Hero Boy (his actual given name is never used in the film either).

Garfield's Halloween Adventure, 1985, frightened a generation with an old fellow in a shack whispering a warning as midnight strikes: They're coming, they're coming, they're coming. Fans spent decades crediting that voice to Orson Welles, who had nothing to do with it; the credited storyteller is Pat Carroll, later famous as Ursula in The Little Mermaid.

And the argument that never ends: Die Hard, 1988, happens at a Christmas party, and at his 2018 roast Bruce Willis declared that Die Hard is not a Christmas movie.

arcade-golden-age.context_blurb:
The quarter-munching era opens in 1972, when Atari dropped two paddles and a bouncing square into bars and pizza parlours: Pong. The co-founder who ran that project, and who later built the pizza-and-animatronic-mouse chain Chuck E. Cheese, was Nolan Bushnell. Five years on the arcade came home in a wood-grain box from Atari, which called the machine the VCS (Video Computer System) until the 5200 made it the 2600. One cartridge hid the first known Easter egg, a programmer's name walled up in a secret room: Adventure. Another, a shooter about a fly gnawing at a force field, ran a band of boiling static down the middle called The Neutral Zone. Nearly all of it thought with the same cheap eight-bit brain, the MOS Technology 6502.

Japan answered in 1978: Tomohiro Nishikado's marching aliens emptied pockets so fast that the country was said to run short of The 100-yen coin. In 1980 the pizza with one slice gone gave Namco's Toru Iwatani his hero: Pac-Man, who is Yellow and hungry and hunted by Four ghosts; the aggressive one who takes the shortest path is Blinky. Boston students at General Computer hacked the board into a bootleg called Crazy Otto, and once Midway licensed it the hack became Ms. Pac-Man; the engineers were Doug Macrae and Kevin Curran. Namco's swooping-formation line ran from Galaxian in 1979 to Galaga in 1981, which hides the most patient secret in the arcade: spare The blue aliens at bottom — The two blue aliens of the bottom row — fire nothing for a quarter of an hour, and the fleet never shoots again. Namco also buried a pump-wielding digger in colored dirt: Dig Dug.

Nintendo's turn came in 1981. Shigeru Miyamoto wanted a sailor, his sweetheart and a bully from the funny pages, Popeye, lost the licence, and built his own ape instead; the woman on the girders is Pauline, and the carpenter was renamed Mario (after Mario Segale) by the 1982 sequel. The Famicom opened in Japan with three ports: Donkey Kong, Donkey Kong Jr., and Popeye.

The Midwest built the hard stuff. Stern's talking maze-shooter with the unkillable bouncing smiley was Berzerk. Williams handed Eugene Jarvis the sideways rescue shooter Defender, whose panel demanded Five buttons plus a two-direction joystick, and then the twin-stick meat grinder Robotron: 2084. John Newcomer made the flap-to-fly duel Joust, player one on an ostrich and player two on a stork, with buzzards under the enemy knights. Atari drew Asteroids in glowing vectors in 1979, and Centipede's trackball came from one of the era's few women designers, Dona Bailey. Konami walked a frog through traffic in Frogger, whose home port shipped with a bonus: Parker Brothers gave away free Frogger 45 RPM records with the game. Gottlieb's long-nosed orange hopper cursed in punctuation, A cartoon-curse symbol cloud (@!#?@!).

Then the counters ran out. Pac-Man's fruit table overflows at Level 256; Donkey Kong's bonus timer breaks at Level 22. The 1983 crash sent two Atari embarrassments into a New Mexico landfill: the movie tie-in, and Atari 2600 Pac-Man. Score chasing filled the silence. Billy Mitchell ate a perfect 3,333,360 in 1999 at Funspot in Weirs Beach, NH, answered Steve Wiebe's million with a couriered tape of 1,047,200 in 2007, and lost the record in 2018 when Twin Galaxies' chief Jace Hall showed the tape came off an emulator. The era's ghost story is the Portland cabinet that men in suits are said to have carried away, Polybius.

Later quarters bought more. Sega's Yu Suzuki gave OutRun a Ferrari, a radio and forking roads, and the deluxe cabinet added A hydraulically actuated motion seat that tilted the player with the car. Midway's NBA Jam took its burning-hot holler from announcer Tim Kitzrow, and the Tournament Edition hid Bill Clinton in the secret roster. Konami's four-player Simpsons brawler tucked an extra life Behind the bowling alley garbage cans, and its rhythm games wore the brand Bemani. Hollywood paid the favour back: The Last Starfighter rendered its space battles on The Cray X-MP supercomputer, and Wreck-It Ralph seated its villains in a circle chaired by Clyde (the orange ghost).

nintendo-console-games.context_blurb:
Nintendo's 1983 Famicom became the grey American machine of 1985, and NES stands for Nintendo Entertainment System. Each licensed box carried a gold badge reading Official Nintendo Seal of Quality. Cartridges needed a lockout chip to boot, the 10NES. The pack-in game that showed America what the machine could do is Super Mario Bros. Its plumber in the red cap is Mario, and the fire-breathing turtle king who carries off Princess Peach is Bowser. Miyamoto set the first Goomba beside the first question-block so a child learns at once that Goombas hurt on touch and die from a jump. His co-designer on that game and on Zelda for forty years is Takashi Tezuka. Nintendo's first staff composer, who wrote the Mario underground theme and the Zelda overworld, is Koji Kondo. The World 1-2 warp pipes send Mario to worlds 2, 3 and 4. Clipping past that wall instead drops him into the Minus World. On the Famicom Disk version the same clip gives three different glitch-worlds, and one can actually be finished.

The green-tunic, elf-eared hero is Link, and the kingdom he saves is Hyrule. The 1986 Famicom game with a save battery inside the cartridge is The Legend of Zelda. America got it on a gold cartridge, as did Zelda II: The Adventure of Link. The Famicom's second controller had no Start button but did have a microphone. Metroid's orange-suited bounty hunter is Samus Aran, and a fast finish revealed that Samus was a woman. The D-pad, the Famicom and the Game Boy all came from one engineer, Gunpei Yokoi. His grey 1989 handheld with the green screen is the Game Boy.

Tetris was written in 1984 at Moscow's Soviet Academy of Sciences, its name taken from the Greek for four. Its programmer, who saw no royalties until the rights reverted to him in 1996, is Alexey Pajitnov. The publisher who flew to Moscow and dealt with ELORG for Nintendo is Henk Rogers.

The SNES launched in August 1991 with a cape, a green dinosaur and a pack-in cartridge, Super Mario World. Yoshi's concept sheets gave him a joke Latin name: T. Yoshisaur Munchakoopas. Star Fox in 1993 carried a 3D chip inside the cartridge, the Super FX. America's Super Mario Bros. 2 was a reskinned Famicom game, Yume Kojo: Doki Doki Panic. The real Japanese sequel reached the West in 1993 on Super Mario All-Stars. Squaresoft's 1987 last-chance role-playing game was Final Fantasy. Hironobu Sakaguchi would otherwise have gone back to Yokohama National University for an engineering degree. Chrono Trigger's characters were drawn by the Dragon Ball artist Akira Toriyama. Its score is Yasunori Mitsuda's, written until a perforated stomach ulcer from overwork put him in hospital.

The N64 controller's three prongs existed for its new middle grip, the analog stick. Nintendo's marketing bragged about a 64-bit processor, twice the bus width of its 32-bit rivals. The Rumble Pak ran on two AAA batteries. Super Mario 64 hides 120 Power Stars, and Bowser dies after three tail-tosses into the bombs. Speedrunners skip the castle by building negative speed against a wall: the Backwards Long Jump. Mario Kart 64's flat, hazard-free battle arena is Block Fort. Smash 64's four unlockables were Captain Falcon, Ness, Jigglypuff and Mario's brother; Marth arrived with Melee. Melee players found an unplanned slide out of a diagonal air-dodge and called it wavedashing.

Rare's GoldenEye 007 was built by a team of nine under Martin Hollis. Its one-shot pistol is the Golden Gun, its favourite trap is proximity mines, and the banned character, too short to hit, is Oddjob. Beating the Dam in two minutes forty unlocks the big-headed DK Mode. Resident Evil 4 put the camera over Leon's shoulder in a rural Spanish village. Earthworm Jim's creator, later of Catscratch, is Doug TenNapel. The 1989 Nintendo film The Wizard advertised an unreleased game, Super Mario Bros. 3. Mattel's infrared glove for the NES was the Power Glove. Captain N's teenage hero, dragged into Videoland, is Kevin Keene. Mother Brain's voice was Levi Stubbs of the Four Tops. The Konami Code begins with two ups. Its author, who found his own Gradius too hard, is Kazuhisa Hashimoto. Digimon's keychain pets fought for shelf space with Tamagotchi. Nintendo dumped Sony's CD add-on on stage in 1991 for Philips. The 2006 white console with the motion wand is the Wii. The 1998 N64 Zelda that reviewers called the best game ever made is Ocarina of Time. Fans mocked Wind Waker's cel-shaded toon Link as Celda.

sega-sony-microsoft-consoles.context_blurb:
Sega had owned the arcades, and in 1989 it brought a sleek black 16-bit machine to America as the Sega Genesis, sold in Japan and Europe as the Mega Drive. Inside it ran the 16-bit processor that also drove Macintoshes, Amigas and most arcade cabinets of the decade, the Motorola 68000. Its music came out of a six-channel Yamaha FM chip, the YM2612. In 1991 Sega answered Mario with a hedgehog whose fur is blue, picked to match the company logo. Naoto Ohshima drew him, and the rolling-physics code that made him feel fast was written by Yuji Naka. The two-tailed fox who joined in 1992 goes by Tails, but his name in the games is Miles Prower. The 1994 Knuckles cartridge carried a slot of its own on the top, so plugging the mainline sequel into it gave one combined game, Sonic 3 & Knuckles. The brawler Streets of Rage sounded like a nightclub because its score came from a composer of twenty-four, Yuzo Koshiro. The mushroom-shaped booster Sega rammed into the Genesis slot in 1994, and killed within a year, was the Sega 32X.

Sony arrived in 1994 with a grey machine that read CDs and put four shapes on the right of its controller: the PlayStation. The engineer who had built the Super Nintendo's sound chip, then talked Sony into going it alone after Nintendo walked out, is Ken Kutaragi. At the 1995 trade show Sega announced the Saturn at three hundred and ninety-nine dollars; Sony's man walked to the microphone, said his own price, and left. That price was $299.

Naughty Dog supplied the console's mascot in 1996, an orange marsupial in blue jeans smashing crates: Crash Bandicoot. The studio had been founded in 1986 by two Michigan classmates, Andy Gavin and Jason Rubin. Crash's exaggerated takes were modelled on Looney Tunes, and on Tex Avery above all. Core Design's tomb-robbing archaeologist of the same year, with the braid and the twin pistols, is Lara Croft.

Capcom invented survival horror on that console in 1996, under a director who later made Resident Evil 4, Shinji Mikami. Konami's 1998 stealth game about a soldier sneaking into an Alaskan base was directed by Hideo Kojima. Its telepathic boss, Psycho Mantis, was reading the controller, so the way past him was to move the plug from Port 1 to Port 2, and he taunted the player by reading the memory card for other Konami saves. The industrial score for Konami's 1999 horror game in a foggy town was written by Akira Yamaoka. Its 1997 Castlevania turned the series into open-castle exploration behind Dracula's half-vampire son, whose name is Dracula backwards: Alucard.

Squaresoft moved Final Fantasy VII to Sony in 1997 because the game would not fit on a cartridge, and the box held three discs. Shinra's glowing-eyed super-warrior programme is SOLDIER. Summon Materia, the orbs that call up Ifrit and Bahamut, are red. Nobuo Uematsu built the final boss theme round a Latin chorus he borrowed from a composer he names himself, Carl Orff, whose 1937 setting of a thirteenth-century Bavarian songbook, Carmina Burana, supplies the words.

Sega's last console reached America on 9 September 1999, a date the whole campaign was built on. Every controller took a memory card with its own small screen and buttons, the Visual Memory Unit. Every unit shipped with a modem, and the service they dialled into was SegaNet. Its first fully 3D Sonic game was directed by two Sonic Team leads, Yuji Naka and Takashi Iizuka.

Sony's 2000 follow-up played DVDs, outsold every console in history, and was the PlayStation 2. Microsoft's first machine, a chunky black box with a green logo, arrived in 2001 as the Xbox. Its launch shooter came from a Chicago studio that had made its name on Macintosh shooters, the Marathon trilogy. The armoured soldier it stars is Master Chief. His companion Cortana was flash-cloned from the brain of the scientist who ran the Spartan programme, Dr Catherine Halsey. Jen Taylor has voiced Cortana since 2001. The long, dim, repetitive Flood level everybody complains about is the Library, and the closing Warthog escape up the collapsing ramp is the Maw.

fighting-games.context_blurb:
The fighting game as everybody knows it starts with Capcom in 1991. Street Fighter II put eight world warriors into one-on-one duels, each with special moves hidden behind joystick motions, and the one everybody learned first belongs to Ryu: hands cupped at the hip, thrown forward, a ball of blue energy, done with a quarter-circle forward and a punch, and it is called the Hadoken. The same game gave the genre its first playable woman, a detective from Chinese Interpol in a blue cheongsam, with hair in ox-horn buns and spikes on her bracelets, whose rapid kick is the Hundred Rending Legs, and she is Chun-Li. Akira Yasuda designed the costume out of Chinese opera.

Midway answered from Chicago in 1992 by filming real actors and digitising them into sprites. Mortal Kombat's selling point was the gruesome finishing move, and the name for it is the Fatality. When a beaten opponent stands swaying, the announcer's two words are Finish him. You then had about five seconds to enter the right sequence. Those Fatalities put the game in front of a United States Senate hearing, which is where the ESRB ratings came from in 1994. Home ports split the difference, since Nintendo's version removed the blood while Sega's hid it behind a six-button code typed at the title screen, and the code was ABACABB. It is a nod to the band Genesis and their 1981 album.

Arcade rumour was half the fun. A green ninja could be fought on the Pit stage in the first Mortal Kombat under conditions nobody could quite confirm, silhouettes crossing the moon and flawless rounds and no blocking, and that character is Reptile. Capcom did the same thing in 1994 in Super Street Fighter II Turbo with a hidden boss, a dark-energy master who is the brother of Ryu and Ken's teacher Gouken, and he is Akuma (Gouki in Japan).

Namco, the Pac-Man studio, took the genre into three dimensions in 1994 with a family feud among the Mishimas, cruel grandfather Heihachi, his son Kazuya and his grandson Jin, plus oddities like the ghost-samurai Yoshimitsu, in a series whose name means iron fist: Tekken. Sega's Virtua Fighter had reached 3D first, in 1993, but the home port made the difference.

One footnote for completists. Disney's Wreck-It Ralph in 2012 put real game villains into a support group, and the studio got permission for the characters but not for every original voice, so one of them had to be dubbed fresh: Kano (Mortal Kombat) — his original arcade-voice was not licensed. If competitive gaming interests you, all of this still runs, every year, at Evo.
